div.head: LADIES' LETTER\
div.p: LADIES' LETTER\
MY Dzeu Nxuar.,

I cannot help but think that many of the new hats make the wearers look top-heavy. This is a fault associated with over-trimming. Over-height also threatens us. There is a kind of wildness in those hats that have a bush of flowers or a great bow of silk jutting out at one side above the temple. When this sort of trimming is applied to a hat of the kind that is bent inwards all round the brim in irregular curves it can look very mad indeed. Still, there are faces that are well-suited with this eccentric, quasi-unstudied kind of head- gear, which matches the "wind-blown hair" so dear to the poet and the novelist. The softness of the new straws is attained by weaving in plaits of crepe alternately with those of straw. Tuscan hats are to be worn when summer comes. Some of them are three-cornered in shape, and projecting in front the brim makes a pleasant shade for the eyes in sunny weather. It is a great error in art when the whole of the trimming swoops forward, with nothing beyond the straight line of hair at the back and a meagre bit of hat-brim. One sees this constantly, however.

arm flannel blouses are the most appropriate for icy wind and a temperature of 30 deg. in the open air. Some of these are pretty enough with Paisley designs or Japanese patterns in good shades of blue on white or cream, or of amber and preen and brown. The addition of a warm velvet bolero over these is not at all superfluous when the chill Nor'-Eater is about, intruding at every think of window and rushing in uproariously at every opened door. A blouse made of viyella was spotted with mauve and lined with plain viyella. The revers and cuffs are black lace, while the waistcoat and epaulettes are mauve silk stitched with silver thread. The tucked silk chemisette and the silk under-sleeves are lined with the plain viyella. Black tucked glace is by far the most fashionable material for blouses, boleros, and short coats, as well as for hats.

Tailor-made gowns are never absent from the wardrobe of the well-dressed woman. Two I have seen are very good at; lea. One in grey frieze it strapped with narrow bands of fintN heliotrope cloth down the crossed bodice and round the skirt. The bodice is fastened by tabs and large silver buttons over a shirt of tucked lawn. The other frock has one of the new long-tailed coats, cut sway in the front, with revers, tabs and a collar of linen lace, which also borders the skirt. The front is worn open, but may be closed by means of the small buttons which run in a close set row dow4, the edge of the cost.

Some sunshades are of white or very delicate. tinted silk, with wide border of chine floral design, and a band of the same round the ferule, and are lined with chiffon, and finished at the edge with a broad band of lace. Handsome black shades are lightly embroidered all over with gold thread, some exhibiting ornate medallions of chine silk set among the embroidery; others displaying birds and buttao. flies worked in gold thread awl sequins; and a sunshade in the most perfect taste is of black satin, veiled with gold-embroidered guipure in a soft ecru tint, and lined with chiffon. Simple but effective shades are of moire or glace silks in charm- ing colours, with a hot-der of narrow black and white stripes, and a bow to match on the enamel- led stick.

A charming gown was made of pale silver-grey silk poplin, trimmed with silver lines and black velvet. The underskirt was made of pale grey peau de sole, and a border of the same silk was attached to tho over-skirt by silver tinsel passe- menterie, with buckles and bows at intervals. The pointed belt was cut in one with the skirt, and had black velvet bows back and front, and rows of small silver buttons at either side. The revers and cuffs were of white glace silk embroidered with silver tinsel, and the vest and puffings at the wrists are of fancy printed gauze with insertions of creamy lace let into them.
Your loving JENNIL

becoming crusted, keep an oyste-r-shell in it. All the chalk that is in the water will attach itself to the shell, which can be removed in due course, and • new one substituted for it. CRACKED EGGS. —A cracked egg is usually con. sidered unfit for boiling in the ordinary way, but if you put a teaspoonful of vinegar and a salt- spoonful of salt in the water it will cook quite as well without the white boiling out. To make a steak tender, let it lie for an hour before cooking on a dish on which you have put two tablespoonfuls of salad-oil mixed with one of vinegar; turn it once, so that both sides may be covered with the mixture.

In the Royal Household a number of changes and economies are to be effected, an rhar the Drop ,aed ii - crease of the Civil List from £.385,000 to £470,000 will not be so great as it appears. The Duke and Duche,,s of Cornwall and York for instance will rec^ive only £30,000 from the Consolidated Fund, whereaa, in 'the last reign, the Prince and Princoss of Wales had £6O 000. The salaries of several of the offlers of State are to he reduced, and the post of Governor of Windsor CaAtle is to be abolished. The Lords in-waiting are also to he re- duced from seven in number et £7OO a year, to five at £BOO. Those who come after the present holders, will scarcely anpreciate the change 8 to be eft cted in these various( Ricer'. The reforms ,xend to bath high and low alike, as the office of Chief Painter, who hag £39 a year, is to be abolished, and even the sum set apart for the housemaids at the Rlyal Palaces,is to be reduced by £205. ' The Duke of York, of course, has the revenues of the Duchy of Cornwall, amounting to about £60,000 a year —in addition to the provision made by Parliament. Taken 113 a whole, the folks on pleasure bent this Eastertide did not haves tad time, as regards weather. And year by year there is a noticeable improvment in the style ot dress adopted at holiday times,by those girls and women who may be said to belong to the masses. No longer are flaming coloured fabrics, and feathers and flowers of gaudy hues, indulged in, a state of affairs in great measure cue to the women's column which now finds a place in every newspaper, and the almost ! numberless faahion journals all of which tend to improve 1 the taste. There still remain however, many ideas patronised by the classes, which the masses would do well to st ud F—and follow. As reg .rds the length of the outdoor skirt for ex- ample. The very great among women never dream of attempting to walk in any hi ng but a walking skirt, , viz., one of suitable fabric, and at least three to tour inches off the ground. But in town they seldom walk- and those of leseer light and leading, seeing the sweep ing skirts of their more fortui ate eisti r; promptly follow in their wake, forgetful that what is possible for those poroessed of a carriage, is not suitable when walking, or when travelling by omnibus or train is one's only means of getting about. Unfortunately the long skirt for out- door wear is an advantageous mode to dresrmakers and tailors, who do their best to encourage it. In white, a new tint is that cdled champagne, which Is proving distinely more becoming to sallow o.orn- plexions, than the " dead " variety 80 long familiar to us. Loa ely gowns, built of camels' hair cloth, and trimmed with suede, both fabrics in this particular hue, are to be seen at fashionable functions, the headgear accompanying such a toilette being invariably black.— Scaled tulle, so arranged that the scatra of a foil are tuggested is the latest novelty in the millinery world,and laid over a foundation of silver tissue, this produces the happiest results. "I am sorry," she said, “sorry for you, and sorry that you should have so little understood or so soon forgotten the answer I gave you before. Try and forget," she said. "It will be best. Good-night." She stood before him, waiting to be allowed to enter the gate, but, overmastered now by temper, he forgot the veneer of former courtliness, and stood purposely barring her ingress. "No," he said. "You shall not go yet. I ask —I will know—the reason lam treated thus. You say nothing against me; why is there no hope, Grace, unless—is that the secret of it—you have a preference for another man ? " She looked him calmly in the face. "It was not necessary," she said; "but I have." "You are not bound?" "I am."

He fell back at her words like a man staggered by a heavy blow and leant against the gate breath- ing in sharp, pain-laden gasps. Grace watched him treinblingly, amazed and frightened at the vehemence of the man.

Only a moment did the rebuff have its effect upon Low. The next, utterly overmastered by his emotions, he started forward, threw his strong arms about the lissom figure of the girl, strained her to his heart, and covered her hot, shame-blushing cheeks with burning kisses. He liberated her at last, and she stood before him a changed being, her eyes flashing in indignant rage. A moment she stood thus, and he flinched from her gaze as from hot irons. Then she raiet'd the glove she carried loose in her hand and stys. him smartly between the eyes. "Coward!" His silence testified bow well he merited the indignity. But an onlooker of the scene did not view the matter in the same light, for, with a noble brute's complete devotion to his master, whatever the justice or injustice of the cause, the dog, which had lain crouched upon the path, rose and sprang towards the girl, growling at her. With a cry she darted through the gate, the man in alarm calling loudly to the dog. "Back, Caesar, back! Down, sir, down!" The brute obeyed, sullen] and wonderingly, snarling to himself.

"Grace " But she had no ears for him now. He watched her flying through the gloom up the long path to the house, and then, still smarting from the blow he had received, the man strode angrily across the fields, the dog at his heels.

THE LADDER OF GUILT.
BY lILYSS ROGERS, Author of "For Love and the Queen,* "Wedded in Mystery," Sze.
CHAPTER L A..RE.IIIOTED PROPOSAL.

uCooey—Cooey—Cooey t" The dog pulled his head out from among a bunch of tangled furze roots, and pricked up his ears. "Cooey—Cooey—Cooey I " Then a long shrill whistle. The day's sport was over. It was time for home. A. moment's regretful glance at the rabbit-hole he was obliged to desert at a critical moment, and the 'a ni mal, taking to his heels, started off in the direction of the sound.

Beyond a knoll on the ridge of the high down he came up with his master, and followed slowly in his footsteps; conscious of a day well spent, uttering but a solitary bark now and again by way of lingering protest at the termination of the sport. Neither by word nor action did the man take the slightest cognisance of the dog, but marched on. with long strides, a dark silhouette against the red glare of sky in the west. His strong, vigorous, almost handsome face was set in hard lines, and an ominous twitching about the mouth told of a conflict of emotion within him. The two most powerful of the human passions were raging not in opposition, but in apposition, not to the exter- mination of either, but to the inflaming of both. For the more Douglas Low felt the passion of his love for Grace Hendon burning within his breast, the stronger became his jealousy of his cousin, Martin Fenwiek, an inheritor, he mistrusted, not only of the estates of squire Fenwick, their uncle, but also of the affection of Farmer Hendon's pretty daughter. Upon the former of these speculations he was assured, but the latter was not so certain. That evening, however, Low had made up his mind to test the matter by definitely placing his poor heart and his equally poor fortune at Grace Hendon's feet.

He crashed on through the thick undergrowth of bracken and briar of the coppice beneath the hill, and out again into the pasture land beyond. To his left, flanked by a row of tall elms, was the farmstead of the Hendons, the blue smoke from the chimneys curling up and standing out in two tiny spirals above the tall tree-tops. The air was calm and still ; long shadows were noiselessly and slowly but surely wrapping the earth in their soft and sombre folds. He had passed the farm three fields' length, when suddenly, as he dipped into the hollow of a meadow, he saw advancing the object of his reflec- tions. He-stopped before her, and the expression of his face changed suddenly in admiration of her beauty.

Wllst struck one upon first beholding Grace Hendon was the dainty contour of her Egure ; in the finished rounding of every limb, in the ease and freedom of every movement shone the reflection of true beauty, consisting not in the excellence of one prominent feature, but in the exquisite symmetry of the whole. Her face by itself might not, by classic critics, have been regarded as remarkable, but it was a fitting crowning-piece to the supple frame which supported it, and she possessed a wealth of hair, nut brown, hazel eyes that tele- graphed, with every varying definition, the thoughts and emotions of the pure soul within her, and a mouth, guarded by ruby janitors, mobile, eloquent, pathetic, comical, according to the shade of tern- pekament preponderating for the moment. This moment she was light-hearted, gay; the world laughed before her; there was gaiety, -health, hope in everything: in the darkly gleaming after- glow of the departed sun, in the notes of the birds, twittering their vespers in the hedge-rows, in the grasshoppers chirping wildly as they settled down in their comfortable corn stubble for the night, in the contented lowing of the oxen, in the caw of the homeward-flying rook, circling overhead. It was the happiest evening ever Grace Hendon had spent on earth, and the secret could be read in a tiny twist of ivy stalk which encircled a finger of her left hand, though to him who could divine such things the scroll of her happiness was written plainly enough upon her beaming face. But Douglas Low saw not the primitive symbol on the girl's finger, and he knew too little of the language of beautiful expression to be able to interpret the gladsome suf&sion upon Grace's face, though he noticed the beauty of it, and his passion was even more madly inflamed. His eye wandered the full length of her form, and, intoxicated by the inspection, he mentally vowed that come what might he, and he alone, would become the possessor of it.

"This is a pleasant meeting," he began, after a moment's awkward embarrassment. "At least, to me. It would be too Much to hope—" "It is always a pleasure to me to meet a friend," she said,anticipating, and at the same time prevent- ing, the observation she knew was forthcoming. Ordinarill she had dreaded this man, for she was not unaware of the passion he had evinced for her, a feeling which found no strong element of reciprocity in her own heart. Once, too, when his attentions were more than usually marked, she had been obliged definitely to indicate her displeasure. Latterly, however, she had been more gracious to him, and upon this glorious evening, with the exuberant joy bursting within her heart, she could not find it in her to be unkind to the worst of her enemies ; if, forsooth, she could have found one. "And is there no cavalier gallant enough to offer you safe conduct ? " he asked, half in gallantry, half quizzically. "Or rather, has none had the good fortune to find the direction of your path this evening? It is getting late. May so unpopular an escort as I be permitted to retrace his steps, and see you safely to Fenwick Barton?" The manner he assumed, savouring of an old- time courtesy, would have been nattering had it not been that she imagined he was aware of the embarrassment his presence cruised. In such a circumstance, to force his company upon her was somewhat unwarrantable. Yet she thought of her own new-born happiness, and would cause pain to

no one. They walked slowly across the fields towards the tall elms and the curling smoke-wreaths, which were rapidly being enveloped in the darker shades of the evening. Ile was amazed at her buoyancy. She had ordinarily presented to him a reserved, almost uncompromising attitude. Inadept and unperceiving as he was, he failed to interpret her manner ; or rather, misinterpreted it, for he ascribed her exceptional lightness and gaiety to a revulsion of feeling in his favour, and his hopes row, with each yard they travelled. They had reached the old swing gate at the bottom of the long thyme-scented garden. Low rested his bag of game upon the ,post. "You have been kind to me,' she said, simply. "My thanks. But won't you come inside ?" she added, as she noticed he had evidently no intention of immediately taking his leave. "Father is always more than glad to see anyone from the Chase. And there is the old welcome, you remember. Last year's cider has turned out well. Martin--I mean, Mr. Martin, and you used to be fond of a glass in the old day when we went nesting together during vacations. All, you remember ? Well, let us go in." "No, thank you," he said. "Stay a moment, Grace. I have something to say. lt must be said. Can't you see—this silence is killing me. No, you have told me I must not speak, but I cannot, will not, help it. It is more than I can bear to remain silent. I love you. There is no one can offer you a devotion more ardent. Is there no hope, Grace? " He had drawn very close to her, and his hand had fallen upon hers as it lay upon the gate. There was h fierce fire in his eyes, and a half- despondent, half-resentful tone in his voice which puzzled and troubled her. She had dreaded an interview .of this nature for weeks past, for she knew the persistence of the man. "Speak, .Grace," he said, for she hesitated, and slowly 'withdrew her hand from beneath his. She was turning very cold, and the colour had left her face. "I gave you my answer before," she said, very softly. "Your friendship I have ever Aspected and valued. Why, oh, why, do you persist in raising what is only likely to prove a barrier between us ? " "Why ?" he repeated, and his breath came in quick snatches. "Why ? Because there is no happi- ness for lye apart from you ' • because, try as I will, cannot stifle what I feel for you, because "—he stopped a moment, his strong feeling overmastering his control of himself and his language—"because I have sworn that nothing on earth shall swerve me from this purpose. What is there against me ? lam not rich, but I can offer a fair competence. There hever is, and never has been, any other woman in the case; I will—" He was :proceeding to protest the proofs of 'his tiffection, but she stopped him.

div.head: CHAPTER 11.
div.p: CHAPTER 11.
TIIE TRAGEDY ON TIIE MERE.
At the Chase, dinner, by no means a formal meal now that the mistress of the old-world Hall was dead, had been in progress for some time.

"We must apologise for not waiting for you," said his uncle, when at length Low appeared. "You are late. Good sport, eh ? Now, Martz, and I," he rattled on, as Low assented by a moody nod, "had abominable luck. We punted about the whole day and only bagged a couple of ducks for our trouble, and those I shot myself during an hour that Martin left me. to go over to the Barton and settle that matter of the lease with old Farmer Hendon. But you don't look well," he added, looking at Low's pale face suddenly. "You've had no accident? What's that mark on your forehead ?"
"Nothing, uncle," replied Low. "I didn't know there was any mark. Oh, I remember, I struck myself with the strap of my bag."
"Well, you look .anything but fit," said Martin Fenwick. "Here, old man, have a glass of something. You certainly look off c olour. What shall it be, hock, sherry ?"

Low drank a glass of hock and pretended to eat his dinner, but it was a studied effort. As soon as he could conveniently do so he retired from the room, leaving his uncle and cousin to enjoy their pipes together.

He felt racked by tormenting passions—love, hate, jealousy—tinctured with shame at the scene he had created to his own discomfiture. Brooding over the matter in the solitude of his own room, he arrived at an assurance that intensified his misery. It was that, in this matter as in everything else, all through life his cousin Martin had been his successful rival. He had suspected all along thsa Grace's aversion for him was due to the preference she shewed for Martin; but he had never really thought that Martin, who inherited many of his uncle's ideas regarding station and pride of family, ever seriously intended asking Grace, a farmer's daughter, to be his wife.

In his own heart, as a matter of fact, Low considered he had done a condescending thing in proposing to Grace. Her refusal was Mortifying, maddening; a blow at his dignity, his self-respect. And what a fool he had made of himself, too He felt he could never look her in the face again. They had played together as children. His mind went back to the time when, having enticed her away from his younger cousin Martin, he had stolen his first boy's kiss from her behind a wheat- sheaf. She had returned it with interest then. He was the eldest of the three; in those days the tallest—almost a head above Martin at that time— and she had looked up to him, admired him, obeyed him, feared him just a little. For he, being the biggest and eldest, was the champion in the warfaret\against the village children ; he climbed the most difficult trees for the starlings' eggs; he it was who waded deep into the pond to save her kitten from drowning. And at Eton he had day-dreamt of Grace away at the Kentish boarding-school, and vowed that no pride, no position, no difference of opinion should ever cope between him and the farmer's beautiful daughter. The thought that whilst she admired him, looked to him for protection; whilst she confided her troubles to him, and chose him as the champion of her wrongs, she could ever have loved Martin— scarcely a year older than herself, whilst he was fully four years her senior—had never in those days for one moment occurred to him. She had always shewn a marked reserve in Martin's presence, had • shrunk from him—had markedly bestowed pre- ferential favours on the elder of the boys to the chagrin of the younger. Poor interpreter of feminine character and disposition as he was, the bare idea- of his cousin as a rival would have appeared to hint ridiculous. Until—and then it came in upon him like a flash of lightning that perhaps he had been making a mistake—until a certain day a year ago when they brought Martin over the Downs, fainting, weak, shot through the ear by a clumsy Londoner who had handled his gun as if it had been the spinnaker boom of a yacht. Grace was standing at her father's gate as they carried Martin past, and she stepped forward to inquire what had happened. But before she spoke she spied Martin's curly hair ; the colour left her face suddenly, and a look came into her eyes which neither Douglas nor Martin ever forgot. Since then Low's life had been a succession of doubts and hopes and fears. The friendship between Grace and his cousin altered not; out- wardly it was the same boy and girleffection, but- Low knew that the girl had change -a. Still, the suspicion had not become a certainty. At times he thought that the boy was trifling with her, that he meant no good by her, and then he would clench his fists and vow eternal vengeance. More often—and he had harboured the sensation ever since the day of his first refusal by Grace—a great wave of jealousy took possession of him, and that nameless hate which every man manifests towards another who, instead of worshipping at the shrine, but plays and trifles there.

Yet he had never shewn any outward manifesta- tion of the struggle that was raging within him. To-night Martin was strangely quiet and con- tented, and Low's inmost self told him that the cause was the same that made hifn the rejected, the , most miserable and discomfited of earth's sons. His head was racking. The ,place was stifling. He must get out into the open air. To pace the fields, to hurry with long strides over the Downs might free him from the demon which raged within him. - He stepped downstairs, seized an old shooting- cap, took up his gun from very force of habit, and went out. He made his way towart, the back of the house, passing beneath the window of the room in which were his uncle and cousin. The window was partly open, And Low pulled up suddenly at the sound of loud and angry voices within. A' quarrel between the two men was an occurrence he had never witnessed andnever dreamt possible. .0,0" lie stopped a man who had been listening alo slunk away. Low stepped after him. It prov_ed to be one of the men-servants. "What the deuce do you mean by it?" asked Low. "How dare you'? " The man made some lame excuse for his presence and shuffled off. Low was continuing his way when the excited voice of his uncle pronounced a name which caused him to pull up short and listen. "This Grace Hendon, this farmer's daughter, I tell you bey. 1 won't hear of it."

'But uncle, tm already pledged. I'm sorry you should have raised such objections, sir. The girl is in every respect worthy of me and of my name, more worthy than I am of her. Her father's position is a matter she cannot help or influence." "Marry the daughter of one of my tenants 1 I'll never countenance it. You're a fool, boy, a fool, like your mother before you. She—" Martin stopped him. "Silence, uncle ! Say what you like of me, but I will not tolerate one word in disparagement of my mother. It is unworthy of you, uncle." Low could not see what took place, but instinc- tively he knew. His uncle was a just man though a trifle hasty at times. The old man had been suddenly stricken by the sense of the injustice he had been led into in speaking against his dead sister, who had strayed far from the bounds of her set in marrying an actor. Low could picture his uncle extending his hand to his nephew. The harsh, angry voices had died away. A few minutes longer Low stood listening, then presently the blinds of the French windows were rolled up, and the recent contestants, arm-in-arm, stepped out into the path. They almost touched Low as he crouched down behind the laurels in the very attitude in which he had discovered the servant.

"It would not have been my choice," the old man was saying regretfully; "but don't be rash. I had hoped you would not have thought of setting up housekeeping for some years yet. I shall be very lonely when you are gone." row heard his cousin's voice making some reassuring reply, but they had passed out of the range of distinct earshot. Then the full passion of jealousy raped in Low's soul. It was true—that which he had suspected and yet hoped against was true. His cousin, who had stood between him and the Fenwick estates, who had appropriated his uncle's care and affec- tion, had come between him and Grace Hendon. He was tortured by feelings of revenge. The raging demon within him possessed him to do some awful thing. His fingers were clutching nervously. It would have been a relief to have hurried after the two, and, seizing his hated rival by the throat, to have strangled the life out of him. He could have gloated over his death. The very fact that Martin held no animus against him—was proud of him, his superior size and bearing, his prowess in athletics and with the gun, his achievements at college, that Martin held him as a brother, honoured him as the dearest among friends—this intensified his hoe, and would hilt have made his diabolical plan th . sweeter.

Ile waited a minute, clutching the gun, and wondered for the first time at having unconsciously brought it with him. If they returned he would let his passion have the rein. It would be a relief to the terrible strain of hate.
But they did not come that way again, having entered by the door through which Low himself had come.

He strode awaw, away to the distant Downs, and, racked by his thoughts, literally three parts mad with the smse of his disappointment, his jealousy, and envy of his cousin, paced the hills. Away in the far distance, out at sea, the lights of passing ships danced in the darkness, and over to the north of the ridge upon which he stood a lighthouse flashed out its signal across the deep. It was a peaceful night and a peaceful scene, but it was not the one to bring relief to his soul. A wild, tempestuous storm would have saved him. The longing for something, for someone to battle against was strong within him. If only the wind and the rain had opposed him it would have given him solace, and he would have been saved. His every impulse loathed the tranquil serenity of the night. The devil in Heaven is the worst devil of all.

Hour after hour he strode about, until behind him rose a lighter tint of dawn. It was the first thing that had suggested he should return to the house. He began to retrace his footsteps. Strangely enough the storm within him began to subside. But it gave place to no better feeling of relief. The devil was no less devil, only lees human in its manifestation. There had been hope for him until now, for a streak of sunshine and a herald of a better resolve might have followed the storm. But instead came a dull, ominous cloud- bank of hate, of malice, of revenge that would hesitate at nothing to accomplish its worst purpose. He did not know it then, but he had been fight- ing the battle of his immortal soul—and had lost. Why is it that men's strongest outward tempta- tions not infrequently come when the hell within them is already more than they can bear ? The dawn was at its full, and he had come down into the hollow of the basin of the Yar and was making his way through the high reeds when a duck flew up from beneath his feet. He was levelling his gun to fire at it when—crack I—a shot from some other sportsman rang out and the bird fell into the sedge. Low pushed aside the reeds with his left hand and gazed across the little sluggish river, swamp it might almost have been called. To his surprise the sportsman who had forestalled him was his cousin, who, with the squire, was now punting - across to secure the bird. The reconciliation had been complete, then. They had adhered to a yester- day aNangernent to shoot early. Low's gun was not yet fully lowered, and an evil intention presented itself to him. Following its vile suggestion, and without giving himself a moment for reflection he raised the gun slightly and took aim at his hated cousin. His finger did not tremble as it pressed the trigger; he was calm, and coot, and determined. There was not a trace of nervousness.

Crack I And now the deed was done a nameless horror seized him. An instant later it was intensi- fied as he saw, not his cousin, but his uncle throw up his arms and fall heavily back into the boat. His aim, usually so certain, had missed this once. Squire Fenwick was dead, and Martin Fenwick was wonderingly and distressingly bending over his body in the bottom of the boat. Horrified at what he had done, Low instinctively turned to fly. But as he did so he became con- scious of a pair of gleaming eyes staring through the reeds and undergrowth. A low, mocking chuckle greeted his ears. His crime had been detected. (To be continued.)

div.head: " WAR AND POLICY."
div.p: " WAR AND POLICY."

The above is the title of a most thoughtful and instinctive work from the pen of Mr Spent! Wilkinson, the wel:-known military expert of t,",,° Morning Post," and which has been published Messrs A Constable and Co., at 15s. The war etw,, dregs on, and in the view of many people the IBC* of policy is more marked now than ever, so that bffi Wilkinson's opinions on "war and policy" 86(4 be read with interest. The various subjects ere, treated with admirable lucidity and with a turento of touch which does much to carry conviction t° the • reader's mind. The initial article on American Civil War gives in short compass el adequate account of the causes which led to tbew great outbreak, and describes the conduct of tbe war and the means by which it was brought to en, end in a most interesting way. The brief sketcbe' of the celebrated generals of past times are valuable as indicating wherein the strength of great colle manders lay, and the means by wtinth some of thei! great victories were achieved. Mr Wilkineo Vole! of I.asp. _he

reviews some of the tactical problems of Moltke and he shows us the wonderful gra military situations and the extraordinary foret which that great general displayed. Mr Wilkil says: 'The command of an army is a matter character, and commonsense. In Napol( words: In war men are nothing, but ame everything.' Moltke's problems are not conch] evidence as to character,but no one can study t without recognising the master quality of n What is visible is the perfection of commonse The graphic account of a vi,it to the Kb' Pass will be of great interest to ti
who remember the time when that wild mon!
gorge was the scene ot many a daring exploit wild affray. He describes the feelings of an Engl man when. he ventures into the native towi

Peshawar, in the far north-west corner- of Indt He says " the looks of the first hall-dozen men Ye: pass give you a new and strange sensation. Ycl° straighten yourself and hold your head up, with. -resolve of which you are hardly conscious till after wards that if a knife is plunged into your back 91 will not flinch. The eyes about you suggest that I there were no cantonment, no others to ask for account of you, your throat would be cut and yoll„,' Icorpse thrown away, and that the people in street would lock on without moving." Mr Wilkia' on covers such a large field that it is impossiole follow him in detail,but his essays on Internation , politics are entertaining and provide much food fe: reflection. He has ?he courage of his conviction' and does not disguise his contempt for the respee!, able non entity in the political world of to-day; thinks party politics are pretty nearly. played 002 and that in any case affairs of national and inter, national importance, should nin be sacrificed 10'' party purposes. That would seem to be a truislill did not experience teach otherwise. Mr Wilkins is net alone in thinking that the nation is badly' need of a few heaven-born state:men to-cteY' There are plenty of political personage: but the " man-in-the-street ' despises them, no thinks he could manage public affairs better hire:, self. Mr. Wilkinson lays down the law with uncertain voice; like the " Honourable George ",°. a few years back he might be accused of being' $ superior person." No doubt he is superior, 11, he has an uncomfortable knack of proving to 11° right. One instance will illustrate this Vintirg 21. national defence in January, 1897, he MakeS following significant statements :—" Toe pre,es Government was weak enough, when it select $ Lord Wolseley as the general of its choice. to Pt him into the strait-waiscoat of a civilian We'' office, and of a council of his own subordinate: Such conditions would paralyse a Napoleon." .10 the light of recent events, no comment is neea 0 on the foregoing. When Mr, Wilkinson touch.) upon the South African War he is equally %/Ow reading; if one does not always agree with b,. one recognises his independence of view and co 0; prehensive grasp of realities. His comparison 4 the war in South Africa with that between Northern and Southern States fwity years ago be recommended to Boer sympathisers in tP„ country. Altogether, Mr Wilkinson is to be CO gratulated upon haviny published a book both ente;s taming and instructive, and worthy the earneit attention of all who have the best interests of tte country at heart.

C suncillor Joteer, continuieg, said he had listened with great pleesure to the statement of Alderman Green, and was glad to 1.-cognise in it a frank facing of the difficulties which confronted them. He felt very strongly as a young member of the C eincie and in this matter some of toe youneer members of the Council supported him, that the Council to- lay, had to fece to some extent the •iifficulties eel by the action of its predecessors. It seemed to him that there was one weak point in the work of the Corporation. As a member of the Assessment Committee—a work which caused a good deil of unpopularity to fall on the shoulders of a few—he weii'd call ettencion to the fact that had it not been for the revision of the assessments carried en during the past two years, the Council would have bad to levy at least another 61 on the rates. no reason why they might not • reasonably expect that this change would produce very satisfac tory results before next year's operation of the Gas Committee were concluded. He was disappointed at the statement of Alderman Honks that trade might be bad for 12 or 18 months to come He was hoping It would improve ' before that time (Hear, hear). The MAYOR said the amendment would practically read that the improvement rate be 3s 2d instead of 3s 41. They could not move a reductioe of the increase from 81 to 61. Councillor A J JOLLKT contended that • the Corporation . ought to meet its liabilities as they came. He hope t the members of the Council would not shrink from teeing the music. It had been suggested that they might do without certain things, but they could net do with- out paying wages, salaries, and interest on loans. and he would like to know which of the scommittees of the Cerpora- tion was prepared to see its estimates further reduced. • liveryoue was aware that the estimates had been very care- fully revised by the Finance Committee and in many in- 'Lances cut down considerably. Great press .re hid been brought to bear upea the committees by their Ilor iugh Treasurer whose services had been very arduous and deserved recognition at the hands of the Council. (Hear, hear.) In the Interest of honest finance he hoped the amendmeet would not b • pressed. Oeuncillor Jolts ROBERTS said that if it was pee ible that an Increase of 61 in the Z was workable he should certainly support the ommdreent. When he found it was proposed to increase the rates by 8d he was almost staggered. Although the rates were bound to go up with the improvements that had been made during the last twelve months. he tnought that if they levied an increase of 8d it would cast a great gloem on the ratepayers throughout the town. Owing to depression of trade and other matters it was a very serious thing for the ratepayers. Alderman KEATON said that as a large ratepayer he should support the resolution. If they had not reduced the rates 2,1 last year they would not have needed to increase them 83 now. It looked mean to propose a rate with which they could not work their way. Councillor BENNETt thought they ought to have a state- ment by the Chairman of the Finance Committee as to what Increase was require 1. lie should be very pleas d if they Could hones ly reduce the rates hut it would be futile to for- get their responsibilities. They must pay their way as they went on. •

Alderman gums said be should like to have an assurance from the Chairman of the Finance Committee that if thy did make an increase of 61 there would be no de iciency at the end of next year. (Ltu fhter ) If there was to be a deficiency they would be in a far worse position than they were at the present time. Councillor Buwros supported the amendnent. fie felt sure they were being saddled with something which they ought not to be saddlel with The improvements were for twtirteytohwoungehrts the benefit of the coaxing ratepayers and he 118 W no reason Ct oh ue lir' oarr:112::::ya added ad supportedt, th toot the ndment. He why the expenditure should not be spread over a few years. pointed out that a great deal of the money seas being spent in they might carry a little forward, and believed that they would find themselves in as good a position if they levied an increase of 64 as if they levied Sd. In Whitecross Ward pathyeetorswerne.r we hhialystinigatothepiaryofworn(vrmaprraoirperrts in other tptertrs4otef had to pay for street improvements. The MaVott said his vote would depend very much upon how the Chairman of the Finance Committee replied to the various points raised He pointed out that if a committee of the high character and the high business abilities of the Gas Comrnitte had such elastic powers of admioistration that it could spend £lO,OOO for the increased cist of coal without increasing the oost of gas he thought it was P eisible for them to boa little snore elastic aod find some contribution to the rates. The accumulation of interest referred to. and which way charged at £1 400, on the estimate he thought could be very properly spread over ea large number of years• Proceeding to deal with the estimates he said there was included a sum of £66) for a new road roller. That was not a renewal but an additional piece of plant and (soul I be charged against capital account and the payment spread over a period of ten years. With these savings he did not think it was beyond the range of possibility that they might be able to reduce the rate by twopence. Alderman l'iloszs pointed out that the G a accounts were made up to the end of March and therefore they could net include any prosp ctive profits of the next year's working in the present budget. The MAYOR said It had ben found in the past that the Gas Committee had charged to the revenue account what ought properly to have been charged to the capital account and r robabiy they might have done the same this year. Councillor TINNIOX said nothing had been charged against trading account which should have been charged against capital. /alderman Sassy Glum in reply, pointed out that they were levying a rate with the certain result of having mc deficit to face at the end of the year, but a deficit they thought they could faithfully meet hereafter.He proceeded to show that it was impossible to cut down the estimates further in order to meet the wishes of those Who had supported the amendment. There was not a man present wh3 did not feel the very serious responsibility of having to Ask the ratepayers for an . increased rate of 8d in the Z. But it nad to be if they were to do their duty honestly. The amendment on being put to the meeting was lost only ICouncillors Malkin, Plurepton, Peacock, W Roberts and the Mayor voting for it. The original motion was then carried and the Council rose.

THE National Union of One Education Teachers has once more pro. Authority. nounced in favour of the creation of one local authority for education, elected by the ratepayers, and raising and paying out local rates to "all schools within the area." The idea is rather captivating, and it may be assumed that it will please the people who want to see the School Board dethroned and local rates paid to di:o nominational schools of all ginds. The rage for this kind of uniformity is more common to the teachers than to any other class, but it does not provide the uniformity all round that would make it equitable and workable. If there is to be one general authority, leaving each school to come to its own decision as to the ainouat and nature of the religious teaching to he given, there 3ught also to be one general auttiority over all the training schools tor teachers, and provision made so that nonconformist teachers should receive proper training in some State-aided college, or else all the training colleges should be remodelled. Uniform- ity of salaries would follow any big-area manage- ment. It needs to be supplemented by uniformity lof educational training. But we do not believe 11 that the Nonconformists will consent to any system that involves paying rates to schools teaching different and c mtradictory religiouS creeds. We should regard that plan as reaction- ' ay, as likely to lead to much religious friction, and as amounting to the local endowment of purely proselytising institutions. It is theoreti- cally plausible, but would work badly, and it would end in the destruction of uusectarian educatioa altogether, which we do not think either desirable or wise. The denominational schools would not be managed by a representative body, and they would be assisted by the rates. Started for a special par. 11 pose, as soon as the working expenses were pro' curable from the rates the religious bodies inter. ested would be relieved, all subscriptions would cease, and they would be placed in unfair core' petition with other schools. The small School Boards would all be swept away in the rural die" tricts. The teachers admit this, and rejoice the fact. They are so mtent on getting better salaries that they see little else. There 0 another aspect of the nnstter that is even more objectionable, Ail the motley fn. education ob- tained from the Sao and from local rates is t° be administered by this central body, and all the increases are to come from tile rates, and not foal any ether source. It was stated that "it was onli possible to get increased muds for educational pot: poses through local rates," and that" the prescov dual system led not only to mismanagement, bclt to extravagance." Tile whole suhj-ict of one great local authoritS7 for elemantary,s,,c indary,and tech.; nical education wants more thinking out before Iv can be considered feasible. The Government plf° is to take the County Council; the teachers' pia° is to leave it to tlito election "of the peoi;le in th° area affected. At preseet there are grave ()We: Lions to either scheme. A revolution of this kW' cannot be defended OA them ground that it wou be a good thing for-theleachers or a good Obi: for schools teaching cr'cietls: It has to be shoW that it would be better for th, ,:liddren, and Ore there is no evidence.

Taxes, Direct ana THERE is a contro- Indirect. versy arising as to whether we ought not to reform our entire system of taxation and arrive at some new principle by which direst taxes should be kept in reserve for times of emergency. The Country was invited in 1574t0 abolish the income- tax, and it declined to do anything of the kind. It would again refuse to return to a large indirect sYstem, because it would sacrifice all the advan- tages we have gained by abandoning the system eft by the financiers of the first third of the eon- tnrY• An increase of indirect taxation would be resisted, because it means restraint upon the industry, and industry has benefited by removing these restraints. The indirect tax opens the door to every variety of fraud and of oppression known to the public, and it must be balanced by a direct tax, or it becomes a system for the relief of the rich at the expense of the poor. The direct tax is theoretically fairer than the indirect. A man knows what he is paying and he becomes interested in expenditure. He cannot be bamboozled by that delusive phrase:about " taxing the foreigner." He is not seduced into the miry Ways of Protection. But our system is a corn- Promise, and it cannot be changed without more genius at the Exchequer than we have had for Beveral years. Mr GransroNs could have changed it. Sir M Mc:Ks-BEACH is quite unequal to the task. As long as he did not disturb the system Sir IV Haacomtr left behind him he did well, and he had surpluses. But he made no reductions, he remitted no taxes to the people, and he went on °Pending or anticipating his surpluses, so that When the war came he was left in an unpleasant Position. He has increased direct taxation to the extent of about eight millions, and indirect to the extent of some ten or twelve millions. How is he te' scheme so that he can obtain ten or twenty Millions of money by additions to indirect taxa- ,tien ? That is the problem. Of course 4 involves interference with trade, and every plan of this kii.d impairs trade, instead of improving it. The exigencies of expenditure may compel temporary additions to be remitted when the pressure has ceased. But if we are to face growing expenditure all round we may have to enlarge our revenue-produc- ing imposts. The increase of expendituve of late apart from the war, has not been normal. We are not sure that all of it has been wise. Expenditure follows policy, and it is conceivable that the coun- try might prefer to change the Government rather than see expenditure going up by leaps and bounds and our general system of taxation altered to a In'lre indirect basis in order to pay our way. The subject is a large one, and it cannot be debated Within the compass of a short article. The public raind must be enlightened, however, and we make iaold to say that no adequate reasons are given either why we are to have e,norrnous expenditure, apart from the war, or why we need make radical Changes in our indirect taxation to meet it. Some new sources of revenue may be desirable, and they aught to be direct and indirect; but resistance is emtain to any large scheme of raising more of °Mt revenue by taxes on trade and food.

i The literary correspondent of one of the morn- papers has unearthed a document issued by Zasrs Min.lie thirty years ago—the list of those k 8 of which it might be said at that time that Cwei„ y copies are in circulation." He studied it, it"B43,s, at the British Museum, where he picked h 11,p accidentally whilo waiting for the volumes epad demanded from the librarian and so inter- ,f`"g and so instructive are its contents that it n .—etns quita a happy chance that the reading-mom 'maistants should have been, perhaps, a little less Prompt than usual that morning in attending to the wishes of readers. What were these books Which were in such demand thirty years ago ? The list is so short that it can be given in full. They were in fiction "PhineasPhinn" and "He Knew He Was Right" (A Trollope), "Ursula's Love-Story" (Gertrude Parsons), "Roland Yorke" (Mrs 4TIII, Wood), " Breezie Langton" (Hawley gra4n) and "All But Lost " (Henty) ; Sir Ri,,Tnel Baker's "Cast Up by the Sea," and stA)n's translation of " Krilof's Fables. In Jiscellaneous literature there were Mr. Gladstone's m uvcntus Mundi," Mr. Lecky's "European la ?tale," Mr Ruskin's "Queen of the Air," "Greater ip,tain," by Mr. (now Sir Charles) Wentworth b, and Dean Hook's "Lives of the Arch- IshoPa " ; and in poetry Browning's "The Ring ad the Book." It may be wondered whether a Sinlihir list issued this publishing season would !liter thirty years' time contain so ma.iy books still 4 iown and appreciated, whsther the titles of the '"lurnea of which the 'Aeries now have " many copies in circulation," will thirty years hence have „Bo familiar a ring in the ears of cultured readers. ".I the whole, as the correspondent in question concludes, the list gives an impression that for a !look to have ultimate reputation as well as con- unnporaneons success is not so rare an event as it ill sometimes said to be.

The idea is to convey a submarine Itesa.thel to the edge of the ice floes, and there sink continue the adventurous journey at the depth rborne hundred feet or so, clear under, it is be.. )ved, the deepest pack ice, though at the mercy th of icebergs, which often go down to a much eater depth, and of any submerged rocks there ZY happen to be in those necessarily unexplored thlters. The scheme largely depends on the "ory of an open Polar Sea, which has long h,"41 held by geographers, and was to some ,I'hnt verified by Nansen in his dash to the u'thest north. It is thought that if there is aiePen water the submarine explorers may be 'J to make for themselves by despatching a tor- vertically at the ice-pack a way upwards ti,l:?ugh the debris, while at worst they can retrace Course to the opening which they left. After, 41'wever, the demonstrations which have been ii ige of to difficulty of steering the submarine `er water, the impossibility of keeping such a cnt even as would enable the voyagers to 4rtaln whether they were closed in above by .0 f.u? or Whether their vessel might rise to the sur- -1 42 for the fresh air which, within a very few would be imperatively necessary, and the t '43' other perils to be encountered,the enterprise da out as so foolhardy in its rashness as to a strew doubt whether it is to be con- ti,,eured, after all, more than an interesting sugges-

"13u1get night" as it is familiarly known signifies holding of the most important of ell the mhly meetings of the Warrinc,,ton Town Conn- zr• On this occasion the local Chancckilcr of the I..,tellequer, Alderman Shaw Green, has his say thic,-8 the liberty of criticising whatever he s fit and raps as many knuckles as come ;4:hin les reach and merit such attention. Lastly, illaPortance first, he announces the rate it 'le necessary to levy upon his townsmen to '''le the Corporation to pay its way. At the •'eting held last Thursday evening there was a ''siderable amount of apprehension in the minds ( he rc•eMhers as they listened to the eloquent 6144/8 °I Corporation finance which fell from the of Alderman Green. Rumour had die- 'c'ed them ei they were by no means le)endn. m at their ease as he deliberately L'ed the many great improvements in hand, ' ~"I"lereus ~ources of vast expenditure,and the , wCent overstepping of bounds by committees. la the Aldermen at last said that "if he knew rri I—ngton people at all, they only needed to be

shown ths reasonableness of a request to grant it," it was borne upon the minds of all,with the fore of an irresistitile conviction,that the silvery words of the flatterer were merely intended to lessen the force of the blow which fell with his announcement of an improvement rate of 3,3 4d in the .C.

A moment's reflection was sufficient to deduce the fact that this represented an increase of 8d in the ' 2 on the same rate for the year just concluded. A cold douche could not have chilled the councillors quicker, and they mimed to listen to the Alder- man's resonant tones as if in a dream, while he calmly proceeded to explain the necessity for the enormously increased call upon the public purse. 11 For some time the spirit of the individual mem- ber appeared to be at a low ebb, and after Alder- man Green had resumed his seat the speeches immediately ensuing were characterized by a tone of sweet reasonableness and philosophic resignation decidedly surprising. Councillor Bennett even suggested a larger increase—perhaps his dream was more vivid than that of his fellow members,— and the suggestion was certainly not laughed to scorn. By and by reaction set in, and follow- ing inquiries,an amendment was proposed reducing the improvement rate to 3s 2d and thus making the total increase one of 6d. It did not receive very much support however, and the original resolution was carried. We think the Council has done the right thing in facing matters boldly. It was, possibly, an error of judgment in making a reduction of 2d last year, and the Council showed no inclination to repeat the blunder. There is no doubt that the present financial strain is in great measure due to the slow, progress made by the predecessors of the present Council. Warrington long laboured under the reproach of being "50 years behind the times" and the efforts made to bring the town on a footing with its neighbours have almost all been compressed within the last few years. An enlightened observer will say that this is to the credit of the present Council, for the town must march with the times, and if it has just now to march at a quicker step than here- tofore we must recognise the necessity and pay, pay, pay ! There is nothing else for it, and we can only deplore that so many improvements are urgent in the extreme, and that trade generally is so bad as to make the burden of an increased rate uncommonly heavy and hard to bear. Possibly the production of gas may presently become cheaper and thus enable the Gas Committee to hand over a profit which will go to the relief of the rates. We do not advanca this hope at all as one to be , depended upon, but merely for the sake of those lwho I@ve to have even a straw to clutch at. One, thing we are convinced of, and that is that rates in Warrington will continue to ha high for a few years to come, until, in fact, electricity, tramways and gas are all contributing to the Corporation revenue. Then we shall have,if not the millennium, certainly better times all round. For those times we must hope and wait cheerfully.

Though predisposed to seriousness the Council did have a little tun during its two hours sitting and that curiously enough was derived from the minutes of the Cemetery Committee. On a plan belonging to this Coinmittee two plots of land are "hatched" (in blue), and one humorous Councillor was so struck with the con- venience of the thing that he sug- gested the Cemetery Committee might "hatch" softie more land. "Perhaps they will, and per- haps they won't," as the song says. Then too, the plots of land in question are iotended for the in- terment of Nonconformist bodies, and this drew forth the query of" which bodies—the Wesleyah, Baptist, or Congregationalist " We imagine a proposal to inter Nonconformist bodies en bloc would create a little ' commotion, partic- ularly if the committee were prepared to " hatch " out lead as fast as it was required. The intention seems to be more innocent however, and the" bodies" need not be concerned about a premature interment.

Concerts and entertainments on the Sabbath are undoubtedly increasing in number both here and I elsewhere, and we are convincea that the results I will not be of the kind calculated to further the moral and spiritual well-being of the people. Sacred concerts—not only sacred in name, but in nature —can do little harm as long as they do not inter- fere with religious worship and they may, possibly, do some good. Certainly the people who attend them are milling better use of their time than they would be in aimlessly prowling about the streets. Concerts such as these are the exception, howevur, and there is many an entertainment on the ,Sabbath glossed over by the adjective" sacred" which is no more sacred than a fourth-rate comedy or drama and has been organised for no other purpose than to make money in a fashion difficult to justify. For instance a company of pantomime artistes sometimes gives a" sacred" concert on Sunday and mouths which spent the Saturday evening in framing jokes and songs of questionable taste are engaged twenty-four hours later in giving a 1" sacred " tone to a concert which is intended to swell the weekly earnings of the company. This sort of thing is nothing more or less than a prostitution of the Sabbath and ought to be rigidly suppressed.

div.head: -EXAMINER, FR I DAY, APRIL 12, 1901
div.p: THE -EXAMINER, FR I DAY, APRIL 12, 1901

It is said that from both England and Ireland in- quiries are received daily, from the heads of parties ranging in number from hundreds to th °mends. For week-day trips exceptionally cheap fares are ,granted by the Scottish companies, and if the Eng- 'ish lines are equally liberal our fellow-countrymen will be enabled to enjoy a fine summer oaring.

The Presidential address at the annual Conference of the National Union of Teachers has, as usual, been the subject of much discussion among educa- tionists generally. The President, Mr James Black- ler,is headmaster of a voluntary school at Brighton, and his idea appears to be that of a national system of education, with local administration. This is a good reminder that our present eyatem is a patch- work. It was not until 1870 that the State became conscious of having a duty to perform towards those children who were not taught in schools carried on by sectarian agencies ; but the law can- not be said to have ever recognised School Boards as having anyth'ng to do except to fill vacancies which these sectarian agencies leave. There is really no proper system of elementary education in this country, and as for secondary educa- tion, that is completely unorganised. It re- minds one oe the story of Lord Kitchener, that soon after he arrived in Cape Town he was asked if be had come cut to re-organise the trans- port system, and he replied no, that he had come to organise it. It is recognized now that there is need for an educational Lord Kitchener,who would really organise,and not re-organise by further patlhwork, the national system of education. Mr Blackler, looking it the Hooligan from the standpoint of an elementary teacher, denies the palpably absurd contention—if there be one—that these rough manners are the result of elementary education, and says very truly, that they are the outcome of street education. The same thing has been advanced at teachers' conferences before and, of course,there is much force in the plea. He naturally lays great but not undue stress upon the benefits to be derived ' from religious. but not dogmatic, education.

Although certain returns have this week appeared relating to various small centres of population, the ordinary national account of the census will not be presented in its completeness for a considerable time, and we shall have to;be content to receive our information on the instalment system, and so to arrive gradually at certain conclusions respecting the distribution and condition of the population. The crowding of the people into a limited number of rooms will be ascertained for the first time, though owing to lack of experience on the part of enumerators, as referred to in last week's letter, not so accurately as might be desired. The public will also know approximately the extent to which the war has reduced the number of men; and whether the unmarried population is increasing or diminishing. Likewise whether the number of foreign-born people among us is greater than it was and whether the rate of increase shown in previous decades is'heing maintained. The tendency of trades to die away and of new occupations to come into existence will be indicated, and also the number of women in independent occupations be shown, together with the nature of the occupations of the dependent classes. Thee will all be found enumera- ted with greater care and accuracy than was ever possible before, and the first census of the new cen• tury should long continue to be a subject of very special interest,

Our coal supply is too big a question to deal with in this letter, but it is one that is again forcing itself on the attention of the public. Professor Jevons. in 1865. predicted that our cellar would be empty in little more than a hundred years, and that a check to our progress would be perceptible within a century of the year in which the prediction was uttered. But the Professor over-calculated the consumption of coal, just as the Royal Commission, five years later, under-estimated it. The question ;pat is being asked now, however, is whether there can be any connection between the elaborate calculations pub- lished in the " Times," on the subject of our coal supplies. and the proposal that the Chancellor of the Exchequer should impose a tax on all coal exported to other countries. The writer of the article in the paper mentioned has taken pains to make the facts very clear, and it will seem to many people that the gradual depletion of our coal measures demands the attention of the nation. By all means let the matter have prompt and due attention, but there is net the slightest evidence at present of any new cause for alarm.

Most readers will agree with Mr Waddington, of Bolton, in saying- as he did at Tuesday's meeting of the National Association of Teachers, that it is absurd and wasteful to have one authority for ele- mentary education,another for technical education, and the prospect of a third for secondary education. It is certainly an adroit way of avoiding a difficulty to provide that a local vote shall decide whether the authority in each educational area should be direct- ly or indirectly elected, although it would be too great a responsibility probably to impose on any I body of electors to decide, once for all, which method shall be adopted It is conceivable that the present Government might be willing to legislate to deprive School Boards of their power, but there is not much probability of Mr Waddington's plan being adopted by the Government, much as may be said to recommend it.

The" Old Folks" treat was duly carried to a con- clusion on Wednesday evening last, but did not quite reach the standard of the treats of previous years, as far as attendance was concerned. Another point that the Committee must in future bear in mind, is that the nature of the eutertlinment for the " old " should be provided by the "young." A troupe of juvenile niggers or " juvenile enter- tainers" would go further to please the "old 'um" than such a h'gh-class programme as was submitted to them on Wednesday' Given something to laugh at, and nothing to over •awe them in the shape of long speeches (which the half of them are too deal to hear) and old people are pleased and thankful.

The Runcorn Urban District Council have issued notice of the deposit of bye-laws for the col:aro' of Ituncorn Heath and at their office, in the Town Hall. The same will be open for inspection by ratepayers. A similar course, too, has been taken by the Runcorn School Board, with regard to the new bye-laws, under the Elementary Education Acts Now is the time the ratepayers should en- quire into these matters, and thug save useless regrets in years to come !

--- A word about the Transporter Bridge. It is ex- pected that building operations will be shortly taken in hand. As an indication, we see that the Lof.al Council, and the WPnes Corporation, have been no'ified of tht first call, and both bodies are busily nogotisting for the required loans to eet the ',sine. Thit news will be somewhat welcome in facs of the slight depression in the staple indus- try—chemical-i, under which both towns are at pre- sent labouring.
The 'Runcorn Football Club have practically con- cludel this season, it will be ray pleasing duty to reviow the season's play in the next issue of this paper.
