div.head: REV A WELLS ATTACKED DY A DOG.
div.p: THE REV A WELLS ATTACKED DY A DOG.

As the Rev Alfred Wells was returning from the Old Folk's Treat on Wednesday night, by way of High-street, a dog rushed out of the entrance to Mr Savage's and bit him very severely. Mr Wells was very much startled, but soon recovered him- self and walaed home. A DISGRACEFUL STREET SCENE.

John Bourke, labourer, a well-known Runcorn character, was charged before Messrs W Handley and I: Imison, on Wednesday with begging in fligh-street, and with being drunk.-I'.C. Bratt proved the case. It appeared that Burke was very drunk, and was staggering about the street with his clothing very much disarranged. He was also making himselt objectionable by begging.—The record against Burke saowed that be had been con- victed 48 times previously, and had only come odt of prison a few days previously after serving a term for using obscene lenguage. lie was not eligible for the inebriates home, so the Bench sent him to prison for a month for begging, and dis- missed the other charge. SAD DEATH OF A RUNCORN FLATMASTRR.

_ An inquest was held on Tuesday, at the Liverpool City Coroner's Court, by Mr T E Sampson, on the body of James Massey, 41 years of age, master of the flat Esther, and who lived in Union-street,Run- corn, who was killed in Duke's Dock on Saturday. It was stated that the deceased took a number of cases of bedsteads to Duke's Dock on the fiat to be unloaded. ile was in the hold putting a sling round the cases in order that they might be hoisted up a distance of about 30 feet. Fifteen cases had been hoisted, but when the next had reached the top and was being lowered on to a truck, it was surmised that some of the bedsteads shifted, which caused the case to list, and fall down the hatch. It fell upon the deceased in its descent, and he was removed unconscious to the Royal Southern, flospital,where he died from his injuries shortly after admission. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," but added a rider that it would be advisabls to construct a trapdoor to ;.-re- vent any load falling back. RUNCORN BOATING CLUB.

"The early member catches the boat." This, as levents :turned out, was evidently the motto of the bulk of the members of the expanding organise- tion, since as early as 6.30 a.m., on Good Friday members were to be seen wending their way to the well stocked boat house at Rocksavage. The open- ing day for season 1901 was grand, not only as re- gards the weather but also as regards the large and enthusiastic number of club members present. 2.30 p.m saw every boat in use. At eventide the caretaker reported that he was perfectly "knocked out" with handling boats, and remarked that it was the busiest day the club had known since its incep- tion. Up at Pickarings there was quite a fleet of boats moored while their crews satisfied the inner man, and while Ashleys were preparing the neces- sary recuperation the neighbourhood's children had a few minutes of frantic delight at the gyrations of a number of boaters w'so indulged in a rough and tumble with a rather emaciat-e:1 rugby football. The score was about ev.n, as also were the casual- ties. An interesting feature of the day was the successful launch of 3ir F Abel's steam launch " Winifred." which had been refitted and generally overhauled during the winter months: Apparently the R B.C. has again started a season which will eclipse its predecessors in every way, PRESENTATION AT CAMDEN WESLEYAN CHAPEL,

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

Mr J W Bayley's society class was held as inual on Wednesday night, at the Camden vestry-room, Lowlands-road, Runcorn. The occasion was, how- ever, somewhat unique. inasmu.lh as the members presented him with a beautiful clock, and his wife with a pair of fine painted placques. Mr Bayley has been a class leader for over 30 years, and a chapel steward. The proceedings were presided over by Mr S Walker, a member of 20 years stand- ing. The presentation was made by Mrs Morris, She hoped that Mr and Mrs Bayley would clntinue to carry on the work at amden, and live on in the good cause for a number of years. Mrs Harrison. Mrs Santley, Mrs Bennett, Mrs Hazlehurst, Mr Boden (St. Pauls) and se ve-al oth• rs also testified their appreciation of Mr Bayley's semces. Mr Bayley, responding on his own and wife's behalf, said his early work started in a cellar in Gilbert- street where an invalided lady lived. Then a school was commenced in a house rented at 2s a week, the officers being Mr John Davies (superintend-nt),Mrs Turner, Mrs Simister, Mrs Evans, Mr E lward Bibby, and Mr Robert Brown. Subsequently Camden chapel was opened and he was appointed chapel steward, a post he had held until a vary few weeks ago. Every contributor—both great and s.nall— who had given towards that handsome present he thanked very sincerely, He would always look upon it with kindly recollection and value it very much, The timepiece was inscribed as follows.— "Presented to Mr Joseph W Bayley by his class members and friends at Camden, as a small token of their esteem of his brig services as chapel steward."

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

This body held its casual fortnightly meeting, on Tues- day, at the Workhouse, Dutton. Mr J Knowles pre- sided, and there wet, also present : Messrs S Woodward J S'okes. T Wright, A II Talbott, C E Linaker, Mclntyre T Darlington. J Nickson, J Sprung. T Bszter, J Mouofield, George Pilln, P Gleave, E A Wallington. J B Chadwick, W Fletch.r. C linylance, E Choke, E Bretherton ; with Messrs George F Ashton (clerk), W E Bough (assistant clerk) ; I Farrington (insnec•ch) ; W Diggle and J Swinton (surveyors) ; and Dr .1 Adams (medical offloer).
DEVELOPMENT OF TR& TRELWALL NUISANCE. THE QUESTION OF AN EXPERT.
Ii the course) a the meeting the following lettere were read by the Clerk : _ .

Legal Government Board, Whitehall, S.W., 3rd April, 1901. Sir,—l am directed by the Local Government Board to advert to previous correspondence with refer- ence to the nuisance arising from Messrs Leng's Tannery at Thelwall in the Runcorn Rem! District, and with regard to the paragraph marked 3 in the Medical Officer of Health's report dated the 18th December lest, I am to enquire what stets; nave been taken as regards (h), (c), and (d) of that paragraph and to remove the conditions referred to under (al. I am to state that in view of the serious allegations which Mr Naylor has enar)e.it appears ' to the Board that it is incumbent on the District Council , to satisfy themselves as to the effect upon health of the effluvium and other nuisances referred to as certainly and promply as possible. I am to reqeset that the Beard be furnished with an early reply,—l am, sir, your obedient servant, John Lithihy, assistant sccretary.—To the Clerk co the Rural District Council, Runcorn." Mrs Elith Reynolds, of M Thelwall, wrote under date April Bth to Mr Ashton the clerk. .—I beg to say that I cnnsi ler he book by the side of the road below Cuerden Hell most offensive and • danger to health, and should he very glad if you would cover it up or otherwise deal with the nuisance. Mrs 3 A Queonall. of Cuerden Place, Waste Jane, Thslwall, wrote under date April 9 h on the same sub- ject :—Sir. Being one that has been affected by the dreadful smells that arise from the timpani bro)k in Waste-lane, I appeal to you with the ot jeer. of convinc- ing you that the people of Tnelsvell are not complaining without came. I can assure you Sr the smella at times are ecimerhing terrible. On several oceasions just lately when I have been passing the brook it haft bean so had is to ^aim me 'o vomit. Several others living close to me are affected in the same way when passing the brook. Ahnut, two months ago ry husband was going to his work in the early morning. De was quite well when leaving home, but when he came to the brook he said he never ha! such a shock in his life. His ehest and throat woe, so effected that he had to give UP work, and coneervently had to send for the doctor. And I do think mew If that the smell of that brook had something to do avi,h the ;Soma and death of Mr. Vickers' fine lit'le by who nied some two or three weeks since. I was in the same 'bus es the child and his mother on he Saturday previous to his illeesa.returnine fter• Warrington. While Passing the brook his m i'her, myself and others remarked how very dreadful the smell was on that day ; in fact we had to cover our mouths as it always seem to affect the throat and chest. In a little over a week from then the poor little fellow WAR dead. I think, sir, this eheuld be eneueh to convince you that it mast be iajorious to the health of the people of Thelwele especi- ally these is Wasterlena, ml we de hope yos will tako some steps at once en abate this dreadful nuisance, as most of us have large families and young chil iron, and are MIRE anxious that something should be done as eoon Ps Pessible tor the benefit of our little ones. jam sure we should all be truly grateful. I have often heard it rematked that the brook was a disgrace to the perish of HrePoenhall, but I think it is nothioe less then a death- trap to the Twinge of Thelwall. Trusting this will have the desired effi ct." The Clerk explained that he had looked up the er'sr,letß referred to in the miter of the Ineal Given- Meet Beard and suhmVed them es follows for the "kismet+ of the gremoil •• Causes of offensive smells (a) In Rummer the deeernpersine Parsee in the open cut h has been the cause of much eft:naive odour (b) The eTking pi's for fresh hiders emir a disagreaahle odour when digt,:v.:rid or emptied into rtlieg tanks from time tn time (c) The drone of 8 i:hines in the renen air at times give, riff, to offen,iy, efllivla (ml) Accumoletion of deeereinesing paitnal and tannery refute emit r &naive effievia if allowed to accumulate too long (e) A general

smell common to all tannery processes in always per- ceptible." Dr. Adams, dealing with the points raised in the Local Government Board's letter, said, with regard to the soaking pits emitting • disagreeable odour, at the time be made his report the soaking pits were discharged in a different manner t what they were at present ; a fact he only ascertained as late as Toursday last. Th? matter now went into one large chamber for treatment, and the disagreeable odour mentioned in the report was to a certain extent obviated. With regard to the second point (c) " The drying of fleshings in the open air at times gives rise to offensive effluvia." He del not tuink that anything could ha done to obviate that, as it was always perceptible in connection with other tanneries. The Chairman: Is it the aame in any other tannery?

Dr Adams : Yea ; you find the same thing in other tanneries. With regard to the third point (d) " Accu- mulations of decomposing animal, and tannery refuse emit offensive effluvia if ado wed to accumulate toe long." He did not think anything could be done,except that care should be taken by the tannvry labourer to prevent the accumulation going on toe long; but even then they were bound to have a smell in the summer- time. With regard to that punt be had seen Sir Lg and explained it to him, and since last summer he (the doctor) had not seen toe same conditions as occurred then.
The Chairman : Then you think the three things are remedied to a certain extent?

The Mctor replied in tho same terms as hls first answer to the questions. Asked if he conoidered the drying of fleshings to be dangerous to heate,Dr Adams replied he was not aware that the drying of fleshings was injurious to health, or calculated to cause zymotic or infectious diseases. He did net think there was any contaminations from the ' fleshings, which caused disease.

' Mr Fatlington asked would not the smell from drying hides which had become practically green with rotten- ness and decomposition be considered injurious to health. Dr Adams explained that" injurious to health " was a phrase of very wide significance, and was supposed to refer to such conditions as were likely to bring about dnseases of the zymotic or infectious character.

Mr Wallington pressed his question. Dr Adams said he was of opioion that tanners did not have for their object the dezomposition ot leather, but, if decomposition was carried to the extent indicated by Mr Wallington, there would be an element of danger. Mr Stokes asked whether the conditions pertained to ' other tanneries ? Dr Adams answered that practically they did. Mr Stokes then thought that the point seemed to be that the Council should get to the origin of the peculiar smell, and if tney found how it origiaated they could deal with the matter.

Mr Linaker added that it had been suggested more than once, that not only was this smell Itljti rious to health, but also iojurious to vegetation, and that trees had been destroyed. He should like to know whether any chemical process was employed, or any chemical gases given off which could be injurious to vegetation. He could say of his own experience there was a smell about the tanyard not very pleasant, and the smell he experienced was certainly not the ordinary smell of a tanyard ; and he tbought they ought to fiod it out. Dr Adams prestinvd Mr Linaker was talking of a different smell being perceptible in the tanyard to the one outside. The smell from the brook—
-- Mr Linaker : lam speaking of the Tannery smell. The e:era pointed vut that the Local Government Board's reference to the brook seemed to call for more attention.

Dr Adams pointed out tie) that decomposing sewage would smell more than anything else, and was a well known cause of both diphtheria and typhoid fevers. Last year the brook contained a tremendous amount of sus- pended organic material most of which decomposed in cthaerropend and icch h .the result Biltisq(tutly some improvements were iecl out, of the last analysis of the • fiLient indicated that it was now practically clear that it: came front the Tannery and entered the brook. It contained pract,cally no suspended material of an organic nature and not so much other matter as previ- ously. 3efore it was described "as unfit to turn into any watercourse " and after the improvements it was desctibed " as fit to turn into any watercourse."

_ Mr Wallington: Waal, the doctor tells us is that the rfiluent is practically purified. If that is so the ques- tion I should like to ask is how is there fermentation 7? Dr Adams objected to words being attributed to him- self which he had not used. Ile did not say the diluent was purified, what he said in substance was that ,it passed the standard of the counts analyst. It was I still sewage ; but sewage of a certain standard. What I Mr Wallington described was net fermentation. Mr Wallington : What is not fermentation ? I be to differ with you. Dr Adams : It is not fermentation: It is only •iie same as if von put soap auks in a bottle and shook them up._ It is froth—simply froth. . . -

!dr Wallington adherA to hif opinion, however. Mr J Mclntyre said there was a Statement abroad,and it had been repetted by some gentlemea present that the , Smell as Injurious to vegetation, Mr Linaker begged to correct Mr Mclntyre. He had said it was suggested. Mr Mclntyre accepted the correction, and explained that there was a tree killed situate where the setling tanks at present stood,but it was easily accounted for by the lime. That was the only tree that bad sustained any injury of any kind. Mr Wallington thought it would be better if Mr Mclntyre said nothing on the subject. The Chairman: Order ! Order! Fhe Clerk drew attention to the portion of the Local Government Board's letter which pointed out that the District Council should satisfy themselves as to the effect on health of the efflavium and other nuisances referred to as promptly as possible. Mr Woodward raised tho question, as to.whether the matter, being a sanitary one, made it possible for any expenses of an inquiry to be charged to the special locality. The Clerk was afraid that could not be done. The only matters they could allocate to the separate parishes were in regard to water or sewage works. The ex- peoses of a general inquiry of that nature he fe't sure would have to be borne by the full district of the Coun- cil.

—Mr Woodward then considered the only way out of the difficalty appeared to be by employing an expert, who in conjunction with the medical officer would go into the matter. but that the cost should be borne by the whole district, he did not consider fair. Mr A H Talbott said he would second Mr S Woodward ,He took it that there was some process in the tanning ' which gave rise to a terrible smell that circulated through the adjacent houses, not only causing discom- fort but injury to health. He thought they should do this without hesitation from the point of view of the health of the union. Be was rather favourable to the charge being spread over the 'ho' e union because it was very likely that other tanyards would come under the same head in the future. (Hear hear.) The discussion as to tne emuloym.nt of an expert was developing when Dr &dams intirna'ed that the bacterio- logical analysis of the various water supplies of the district which had been ordered to be taken some time ago would throw a considerable amount of light upon the cause of the foyer outhreaks• One was condemna- tory, and of the ocher he had only received an interim report which be preferred not to disclose until the receipt of the full report. In view of this fact the Council decided that.the doctor should prepare a reply to the Local Government Board the draft of which would be submitted to the next Council meetlina.

31ILTON P.S.A., WIDNES.

An open meeting was held in connection with the anove P.S.A. on Sunday. Mr J Williams, Harrow, presided over a lair attandance. Miss Lilian Beddows, Bolton, gave several recitations in first- class style and Miss Thomas and Mr J McDonald rendered very nicely several duets. At the morning and afternoon services the preacher was the Rev J Pad lar. THE NEW ORGAN Ar Sr MICHAEL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN. The new organ at St Michwl's Church, Runcorn, will be opened next Wednesday evening, when Mr J T Hughes, assistant organist at Chester Cathedral will preside at the instrument and give a recital. The Lord Bishop of Chester will preach the sermon and the augmented choirs of Runcorn Parish Church and St. 3liefere Church will be in atten- dance. A RUNCORN FLATNIAN'S SAD FATE.

Last Saturday a flatman named James Massey, aged 30, of Union-street, Runcorn, was killed at Duke's Dock, Liverpool, whilst engaged in dis- charging a cargo. It appears that a large wooden I ease fell from a sling and struck the deceased man, inflicting fatal injuries. Massey leaves a wife and several young children. On receipt of the bad news his wife was completely prostrated, and was for some time uoconscilus. MARK MASONRY AT WIDNES. A special emergency meeting was held in connec- tion with the Wilbraham Lodge of Mark Master Masons, at the Central Hotel, last Wednesday even- ing, when Colonel Hall Walker, ML'., obtained the mark degree. At a subsequent meeting of the Allied Degrees, Colonel Walker also took the ' Knights et Constantinople and St Lawrence the Martyr. There were several visitors, and the at- fendance was a large one. The customary banquet followed.

BALL IN AID OF TILE WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB. On Monday evening at the Drill Hall a ball wa4 held in aid of the finances of the Widnes Football Club. There was a large attendance, and the chief patrons were the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman GI and Mrs Neil). The room had been very neatly decorated and at the appointed time the company engaged in dancing to the strains of Mr Gillen' string band, The M.C,'s were Messrs J Fishwick, F Flampson, J Leyshaw, F Murphy, J O'Connor and J Tilley. LOCAL CASE AT THE CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.

Before Mr Yates and a jury at the Second Court, last Tuesday, Robert Harding. of Runcorn, was charged with indecently assaulting Annie Oultram a married woman, of Rock Savage, at that place on the 19. h of Jonuary last.—Mr Montgomery prose- cuted, and the prisoner was undetended.—There ' was a second count on the indictment of common assault.—The particulars have already figured in these columns, and the same evidence was sub- mitted, prisoner pleading not guilty.—The chairman having summed up the jury found Harding guilty of common assault, and he was bound over in £5, and his father in £lO, to come up for judgment if and when called upon within the next six months ALLEGED UNLAWFUL WOUNDING AT WIDNES, On Monday morning, before the Mayor (Alderman G I Neil), at Widnes Police Court, John Phillips, a Runcorn Pole resiaing at 19, Water-street, was , charged with unlawfully wounding another Pole, named Frank Mitchell, of 11, Water-street. From the evidence it appears that the prosecutor • has friends residing in the front portion of the house, No 11, and about 11.20 on Saturday night he went there and remained until 11.30 pm. At that hour prisoner opened the door, and without any provoca- tion struck Phillips a violent blow on the upper lip, cutting it. and knocking out two of his teeth. The prisoner was remanded for a week. FIRE AT A WIDNES CHEMICAL WORN& About three o'clock on Sunday morning a serious firebrbooktetenrutknatowthne Uansittehde maspratt Works." Alkali Company, Wid- nes,Almost as soon as the alarm was raised the works hose pipe was turned on to the fire and word was also sent to the Fire Station, the brigade turning out in charge of Deputy Superintendent Franklin. The fire beat from Messrs Goseage's soap works was also in attendance, and being able to get a plen- tiful supply of water from the St Helens and Wid- nes Canal rendered valuable assistance. The fire was chiefly confined to stock near the sulphur plant, and only a small portion of the roof beeame ignited. The men, however. experienced great difficulty in coping with the flames owing to the sulphur fumes. By about four o'eloek the fire was put out, but not before damage had been dine to the stock and plant amounting to at least £2OO. GREENWAY ROAD PRIMITIVE METHODISTS. On Good Friday afternoon a tesparty was held in the Greenway-road schoolroom in cennection with the Primitive Methodist Chapel. A large num- ber sst down to an excellent repast, which was served by the following ladies :—Mesdames J Stubbs, Eyre, Collier, Misses Shingler, Lunt, John- son, L Stubbs, Peck, Collinge, Hill, and Fleet. After the tea, a lecture was given by the Rev W A E.re to a crowded hall. The Rev J Osborne, M.A., occu- pied the chair. The lecturer took for his subject " Sunbeams athwart fife's pathway ; or, cheerful looks, pleasant werde, and kind actions."—Special selections were rendered by the choir, with Mr W Gittens at the organ. A pianoforte solo was also given by Mr H Ball. The Rev S Wright also delivered a short address. A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, the chairman, and those who had given the music, and the proceed- ings concluded with the Doxology. AN " UNCLEAN SPILIST " AT RUNCORN. Oscar Matison, a Danish sailoreileaded guilty, be- fore Messrs W Hendley'and IS Imison, at the Run- corn Police Court, on Wednesday, to being drunk and disorderly and assaulting one Joshua it Iwo. at the Tidal Docks, Runcorn, the precious nieht.— From the evidence it appeared that Mat ion was paid off at about two o'clock, receiving £l5 for his services on board the large grain- hip recently arrived from San Francisco, U S.A. He subsequently sent for three bottles of whisky and drank one neat. Buoyed up ty the spirits he visited the schooner "C 13.K.P." which bad just made the post and was mooring and incited the hands to join him in a drink. This they did, then it was noticed that If tison began walking the docks and giving or fere to the crew to" man the braces" as if he were the master. Naturally the crew did not ()bey end Nlattison got boll of Rowe (the mate) and nearly suffocated nim by squeezing ' his throat. Henry Moores, canal constable, even- tually was called to the scene and rescued Rowe Rowe, in giving evidence, said matison could scarcely know what he was doing. The Chairman : Did be get hold of you? Wit- ness: Th- whisky got hold of me. (laughter.) 1 [he Chairman; You mean the" unclean spirit " that was within him. (Increased laugh- ter.i—The magi4ra:es fined Mattson Sc and Sc costs for drunkenness, and 5s aid 16s (including the doc- tor's fees for binding him head) for the assault, with an alternative of 14 (tlys.—Prisoner had £5 on his Iperson when arrested.

RUNCORN.

A Life Well-spent. A most interesting event in connection with Sun- day school work took place on Wednesday evening last week in Brunswick Sunday School, Runcorn, when a long-service medal given by the "Sunday Companion" was presented to Mr T.Simister for hie long and honourable csnnection with Sunday School life in Runcorn and Worsley. There are few men who can have given so much time and labour to such work as Mr. Simister, who, at 79 years of age is still actively engaged as Sunday School Teacher and Superintendent, as class leader, and local preacher among Methodists in Runcorn. Mr. Simister was born in the village a Worley, Lan- cashire, in 1822, a time of great commercial depres- sion, when England was in the throes of her first struggles for reform. His family was poor—he being in a very epecial sense the architect of his own fortune. Ilis people were in communion with the English Church, and here young Timothy was taken during his first five years. Then he attended the Wesleyan School from five to eleven, where he received the first seeds of that religious education wnich has borne such abundant fruit here in Runcorn. His education was of the most ele- mentary character. Ile struggled for years alone without a guide, and had to rise at four in tbe morning, when finally a good friend was found to give him a little help in his studies. These studies took place under difficulties almost incredible now, as from an extremely early age he had to go out to help to earn his own living, and every moment for betterment had to be stolen from sleep or recrea- tion. His principal companion in these days was "The English Dictionary." At the age of eleven years, he agaiq attended the Church for some three years, and then in 1836,at fourteen, he finally found a nest among the people called Methodists with whom he has remained for 65 years. He grew in knowledge as in stature and became a Sunday school teacher some time before 1840, but in Mama of the latter year the tide in his affairs was reached, when he was converted, and formally admitted a " member" of the Methodist body. It was some time earlier than this he joined a few old men in a Mutual Improvement Class, where he was the only juvenile member. His early efforts at essay writ- ing were crude and brief, but upon them his after career has been principally built. He continued to labour in unostentatious fashion in connection with the little village Chapel and school for some years. He removed to Manchester, in the employment of Bridgewater Trustees, where he at once found con- genial employment among the Wesleyans there, and finally he was tiansterred to Runcorn in October, 1857, and at once sought the Wesleyan Sunday school—good old Brunswick. The Rev J P "qimner was then in Runcorn, and Sir Dutton had just resigned the superintendence of the school after 27 years service, his successor being Mr John Simpson. The writer has had the opportunity of consulting the old school records, and he finds Mr Simister's name at once placed on them. He arrived in October and found that the scholars used to leave school at about 14 years. fie went to see some of them, and in December started a bible class for these young men with two returned scholars, James Taylor and Harry Lewis; a class which has continued ever since under his teaching —a tower of strength to local Methodism— a reser- voir of righteousness from which the world has been liberally :irrigated and blessed. In January the following year, Mr Simister was anxious to undertake new duties and offeied to assist the superintendent to revive the sick club and to e assist "meant to "do." After 15 months at the school his name was added to the committee, which then had charge of Mill Brow as well, where it lias remained ever since, and from that time no name receives more frequent or honorable mention as Inone has rendered greater or more self- sacrificing service. " Not with eye-service as men-pleasers, but as the servant of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart." He found a society class waiting for him which he commenced to lead on Vi ednesday evenings having then three members—how his spiritual influence has been felt through all these years is ehewn by the experience of this very clue which has now some 70 names on its books,and which is still under his regular and uninterrupted leadership. In 1860 he started a Mutual Improvement Clas, an adjunct of the Sunday School, which met at the member's homes in turn, and when it grew too large at Bruns- wick School. Here also for 41 years be has pre- sided regularly, training the young ideas in intel- lectual as well as moral and spiritual directions.He was quickly placed upon the plan, and his services have for many years been in active demand over a wide area. When Mr. Thomas Hazlehuret began to fail in health, be asked Mr. Simister to take big Fri- day evening's class for three months, then for 12 months, and finally for good, and this he has done for many years in addition to his first Wednesday's class. The topstone of Mr Simister's Sunday School career was added in June, 1878, when he was appointed Superintendent in the room of Mr James Rent, retired through ill-health. The full tale of Mr. Siraieter's service cannot be told now. How he finds time to prepare lessensand sermons—to attend Sunday school and Chapel morning, afternoon, and evening, to lead two society classes, and preside over a Mutual Improvement class mystifies his friends. Neither now nor at any time in this world can the result of these services be appraised. He has given ministers, preachers orators and business men to Wm world in scores; and his only son to the Wesleyan ministry. We cannot say how much poorer the werld would be had he not lived, He is the roost conservative "1 Methodists, can End no fault with its polity. With strong convictions he has often to speak sternly, but be has never lost the re,pect of even his strongest opponent within or without his own fold.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
MINOR OASES.
Warrington Borough Court.
51):41)AI—Before Mr F Monks (in the ehdr), Aldermen Monks, Heaton and Francomo, Messrs. Birehall, Hayward,

S ht and Thornton. DASTARDLY ASIAULT UPON A SISTER —John Winstanley, t 2, Church-street, was charged with committing an aggra- vated assault upon his sister. Blizs Winstanley at 11.10 on Sathrday night and also with threatening Annie Winstanley at the same time—Eliza Winstanley stated that at Le time in question she was sitting in the house with her sister. Prisoner had gone upstairs and objected to them talking. Ultimately he came downstairs and struck hr a blow on the hack of the neck which knocked her off the chair and stunned her for a few minutes,—Annie Winstauley stated that prisoner said he would stop their talking, and Without any warning he struck his sister Eliza on the back of the ear with his fist, rendering her unconsci- ous.—A young man named Smith stated he was proceeding along Church-street tin Saturday night and when passing Winstanley's house he heard screams. One of the witnesses ran to the door and called for help. Witness went into the house and saw the prisoner who was in a very excited state. His- sister Bliza was lying in the chair half stunned and prisoner said he would serve aunie the same. He declared that hie would " Swing for same of them "—P.O Bruen gave evidence as to the arrest of the prisoner,—Snperintendent Afonaghan said he visited the hones and saw the prisoner break a mirror with a walking stick. A window had also been' smashed.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for two months with hard labour.
TCFSDAY.—Before Mr Birchall in the chair), AMermen Shaw Green and Hutchinson, and Dr. Fox,_ .

A FATTIER'S STRANGE CONDUCT,—Thomas Balshaw, of I Winwick, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Birchall-street at 11.90 the previous night, and with assault- ing William Balehaw, his son•—P.O. Bruen said he yr.% on duty in Birehall-street when two of the prisoner's children came to him crying, and said they had been turned oat of the house by their father. It was raining heavily at the time. Witness proeeeded to the house and saw the prisoner, who wail drunk, standing on the doorstep lie attempted to strike his wife and witness took him into custody. Prisoner lived apart from hie wife, who resided in Birchall-street.— William Balehaw stated his father attempted to strike his mother and witness stepped betwetm them and received a blow in the face.—Prisoner was fined Maud costs.

Superintendent Monahan said that a boy named Bilis, in the employ of the company, was passing along Haydook street when he I saw the prisoner leaving an entry at the back of his (the I boy's) employers shop, carrying a vinegar cask. The bac, I stopped him and said "You have beea busing a cask." Prisoner replied in the affirmative and and added that be purchased it from Mr Furness for Is 6d. The shop was locked tip at the time se that the man could not have seen Mr Furness. Being suspicious the boy count-d the casks the next morning and found one was missing. Information was given to the police and he (the Superinten- dent) arrested the prisoner. At first he denied the theft, but aubsequently said he took the cask and brought it back again. The cask. however. had not • been returned.— Prisoner, who still maintained that he took the cask back again was committed to gaol for seven days.

div.head: VOLUNTEER CYCLISTS IN MIMIC
div.p: VOLUNTEER CYCLISTS IN MIMIC
WARFARE.
Novel Scene at Latchford.

- Ac Lriefly intimated in last week's issue, interesting volunteer cyclist manoeuvres took place during the Easter holidays between forces tenet senting the Northern and Southern portions of the North-Western military district. , The Northern force, 350 stronn, and under the com- mand of Captain Abercrombie, 3rd V.B. Cheshire Regi- ment. assembled on Friday at Ashton-under-Lyne. The Southern force, which numbered about 400, acted on the offensive, and assembled at Chester. The manoeuvres at Latchford and Walton and other parts of the district afforded considerable local interest, and were watched by hundreds of people who had been attracted Into the suburbs by the fine weather which prevailed throughout the day. The general plan of operations which had been decided upon was based upon the idea that a hostile army had landed at Holyhead, and was marching towards Lancas- hire with the apparent intention of attacking one or ; other of the large manufacturing towns. An advanced party of cyclists belonging to this invading army was supposed to have reached Chester, news of which was at once sent to Manchester, and thence conveyed to the headquarters of the supposed Northern (or defending) army. The commander of the latter at once took steps to despatch a force of cyclists to reconnoitre and to oppose those of the enemy. The place at which this orce assembled was Ashton-under-Lyne, and the four •ays' operations took place between the two bodies of cycliets working from Ashton and from Chester respect- ively. In accordance with this plan the two parties aesembled at 10 a.m. on Friday, the following being the strength of each :

The section of cyclists hum the Warrington Battalion as will be seen from the abo le statistics, numbered 32, and were under the command of Lieutenant Haslam. They paraded at the Drill Ball at a quarter-past eight on Friday morning, at nine o'clock rode to Chester, where they proceeded to the Barracks and joined the Southern force. They were immediately detailed off for orderly duty, an important work their selection for which was a distinct compliment to the corps. They went with the force to Latchford, aad after taking part in the manceuvres there proceeded to North wich, where they were billeted for the night. The following morn- ing they took part in the operations between Weaver- ham and Frodsham and subsequently proceeded to Chester for the night. On Sunday, together with the other members of the force, they attended service at the Cathedral, and during the remainder of the day they were free to enjoy themselves as they wi‘hed. On Monday morning they left the old city at half-past nine and arrived in Middlewich at noon, a quick spin which showed the utility of the cyclists in war in being able to move rapidly from position to position. They took part in the operations about there until four o'clock in the afternoon, when they rode to Northwich, and after tea took the road for home. They called at Major Roome'e residence at Stretton, and were cmiplimented by him upon the good report he had received upon their con- duct in the tnanceuvres. Warrington WAS reached shortly after eight, and the cyclists were dismitsed a: the Drill Hall.

div.head: FICIDAY'S MANCEITYRES
div.p: FICIDAY'S MANCEITYRES

The Southern force left Chester at eleven o'clock on Good Friday morning and Companies Nos. 1 and 2 were instructed to proceed as fast as possible with the object of holding the Stag Bridge at Walton, the Stockton Heath and the Latchford bridges, and cross the Ship Canal and the railway line, and also Latchford Lock. The Staffordshires were ordered to mar h through High Legh and Heatley in order to prevent anyone crossing Warburton Bridge, and also to keep in the closest tench by scouting with a column on the left. Captain Hart'ere proceeded with his main body (Nos 3 and 4 Companies) as far as Daresbury, where he detailed No 5 Company to crock into Warrington through Stretton, and to com- municate with the party proceeding to Warburton Bridge and with the main boy on the Warrington-road. The Southern force arrived at and occupied all the bridges arid locks at 2.40 p.m., a quarter of an hour before the Northern force put in an appearance. The Southern force retained possession of all the bridges, and a battle, extending for a mile of country, took place from the big bridge at Latchford, the Northern force being driven northwards. The umpire decided that victory rested with the Soothrons. The officers in charge of the 1 Southern force were Captain R L Hartley, of the sth ' V. B. Kings' Liverpool Regiment; Captain Alexander of r the let V.B. King's Liverpool Regiment; Captain VF roan (King's Liverpool) in charge of No 2 Company ; Captain Morrice (let Cheshire) in charge of No 3 Company ; Captain Wilson (Royal Welsh Fusiliers) in charge of No 1 4 Company; Captain Lowe (Staffordshires) Captain Abercrombie, 3rd V. B. Cheshire Regiment commanded 1 1 the Northern force. It would he difficult to speak too highly of the skill which was displayed in the arrangernents for the mimic battles, and the scene at Latchford and Walton, especially in the vicinity of the Stag Bridge, was a novel one the like of which the oldest inhabitant had not seen' The attack and defence were carried out in a manner which left nothing to be desired, the men not only being able to shoot but to ride well, and though the spectators from Warrington and the district were amused at the novel scene it also afforded them considerable pleasure and satisfaction. Warrington was on Friday night crowded with cyclists —volunteets and others—and the town preeented an un- usually animated appearance for Good Friday. Some little difficulty was at first experienced in finding accom- modation for the men of the Northern force at various places in Warrington, but eventually this was satisf aC- torily arranged. The umpires acting with Major Boerne (adjutant of the Warrington Volunteers) were Captaics Hitchen and Strickland, of the Manchester Regiment, and Captain Jacob and Lieutenants Carey and Dixon, of the Bth-40:h Regimental Depot. Theo.) officers, mounted on horse- back, were ably assisted by Quartermaster-Sergeant Burke and other non-commissioned officers from Warrington Barracks, who followed the curse of the rnarceuvres on cycles. SATIIRD/Leg OPERATIONS. -

The two forces of Volunteers engaged in cycling manomvres in Cheshire found the roads in a miserable condition on Saturda7,the heavy downfall of rain having made the going very heavy, Early on Saturday morn- ing orders were issued to the combatants to the effect that the Northern 'force were to advance on Chester, while the Southern men were to hold them in check until an imaginary army from Chester bad come to their assistance. The Southern force, whir* was under the Command of Captain P H Carter, Ist V B Royal War- wickshire Regiment, numbered about 400. and was composed of sections from the Liverpool Volunteers,lst and 2nd V B Cheshire Regiments, Ist, 2nd, and 3rd V 13 Royal Welsh Fusiliers, 3rd V B South Staffordshire, 2nd V B North Staffordshire, and let V B South Lancashire. Tbe other officers with the Southern force included Captain Harley, Adjutant sth Liverpool Regiment (chief staff officer) ; Captain Allender, Ist Liverpool ; Captain Vernon, 4th Liverpool ; Captain Mortice, Ist Cheshire ; Captain Wilson, Royal Welsh Fusiliers ; Cap- tain Lowe, Staffordshires ; Lieutenant Raslam, Ist V B South Lancashire, ace. The Northern force numbered about 250, being made up of sections from the 3rd and 4th V B Cheshire, 2nd V B Loyal North Lancashire, let 2nd, and 3 d V B Manchester, and the Lancashire Artillery. Captain Abercrombie, 3rd V B Cheshire, was in command, and be was assisted by Major Greg, Captain Tlaocoasson, Lieutenants Behrens, Wade, Water- house, &o. The umpire was Colonel Sheringham, com- manding the 22nd Regimental District. Ths Southern force mobirzed at Greenbank, and steps were at once taken to prevent the enemy from advancing by the three roads from Warrington. They took up a very strong position to the east of Helsall village, and two companies were rent to hold Frodsbam Bridge, which was one of the keys to the position while another com- pany was deputed to hold Acton Bridge and prevent the

enemy from advancing over the Weaver. The Northern force showed excellent strategy, and the body defend- ing Frodsham Bridge, after beng hotly attaclod were forced to retire. The Northern force followed their ad- vantage up, and as the result of some cleverly conceived movements cut off the retreat of the Southern men to Chester. Tee umpire accordingly ruled that they had gained the day. On the previous day the victory lay with the Southern force. Owing to the greasy state of the roads several accidents of a minor charac. I ter cccurred on Saturday, among the casualitics being Captain Hartley, who damaged his machine and hurt his band slightly. The Northern force went to Man- chester on Saturday evening, and their opponents to Chester. On Sunday morning the Southern force, accompanied by about 150 Liverpool cadets who are spending the Easter holidays in Chester, at,ended divine service in the Cathedral. The cyclists were played to the Cathedral by the band of the Depot Cheshire Regi- ment, and the cadets by their own band. The multi- coloured uniforms made the scene in the Catmcdral a brilliant one, and the effect was heightened by the pre- sence of General Swaine, commanding the North-Wes- tern District ; Colonel E R Courtenay, chief staff officer; Captain Oxley, King's Royal Rifle Corps, D.A.A.G. ; and Captain Evans Lambe, Highland Light Infantry, dis- trict inspector of musketry. SUCCESSFUL CONCLUSION. _

The operations were concluded on Monday. The! "special idea "contained in the orders issued no Mon- I day rnoining to the Northern cyclists were to th • effect that the enemy's scduts were seen east of the river Dane between Northwich and Middlewich on Sunday evening, prebably looking for a camping ground for a force reported to be at Chester. The Northern forces , were therefore directed to march at ten o'clock and scout over the district named. They were to locate the enemy's bivouac, and—as it was impossible that the enemy's main body could arrive till late in the after- noon—attack their advance guard, drive it back over the Dane, and then hold the line of that stream. The "special idea" to be followed out by the Southern or invading force was that a division had arrived at Chester an Sunday evening with the intention of march- ing on Manchester. The cyclists of the force received the following orders :—" Parade at nine o'clock and march as rapidly as possible by Kalman and Middlewich to Rudheathorhich is about three miles north north-east of Middlewich on the Knntsford-road. Seize the best position there, entrench yourself, and hold it till the arrival of the division, which will be about four p.m. Throw out a line of outposts along the brook from Goostrey t Lostock Gralam station,and send out scouts along the Knutsford and Manchester roads. If you are driven back, retire across the river Dane and hold the line of that stream." The Northern force, under the command of Captain Abercrombie, 3rd Cheshire V. 8.. marched out from the Hulrne Barracks in a storm of rain, which fortunately was of short dura- tion. The country was cartfully reconnoitred, and about noon the outposts of the Souttudm force, which was under the command of Captain Allender, Ist VB., Liverpool Regiment, were encountered in the neighbourhood of Knutsford and Holmes Chapel. Their reinforcements were unable to get up in time, and they were driven back by the superior force of the Northerners. who successfully held possession of several bridges on the main road. Prisoners were taken by both forces, and, finally, the Southerners fell back upon Northwich. A sharp fight took place for the possession of the bridge near Davenham, but the Southerners, for want of reinforcements, gave way, and the bridge was held by a party of the 3rd Manchester. A small detachment of the southern force presently arriv- ed. The men were extended, and it was claimed that they had successfully held the Northerners in check. There was, however, no umpire at hand to decide the point whether matters had thus been equalized. Further reinforcements for the Southern force,consi,ting of about 100 men of the Liverpool and South Staffordshire battalions, reached Davenham a few minut,s before the time which it was arranged hostilities should cease, but too late to be effectively employed. In the meantime the opposing forces had come into action at other points along the river Dane, and an exciting struggle took place in the town of Northwich for the possession of the town bridge. During the fight an officer of the Northern force was made prisoner and conducted to the Angel Hotel. Rudheath, on the road between Northwich and Middlewich, was the scene of another engagement, and there was some sham skirmishing at Rostock. A despatch rider sent by an officer commanding a detach- ment of the Northern force from Middlewich was mad prisoner by the Southerners near Northwich, and aom valuable information wag obtained: When the " cess- fire " sounded a party of the Southern force had concsn trated at Devenhain, and from this point they made the best of their war to their re.pective destinations. Other sections of the two forces followed the same e lure°, and contrary to expectation, there was no gent rat muster of the entire body. The report of the umpire-in-edef Colonel Mainwaring, commanding the 23rd (Wrexham) Regimental Distriet, was not made known, but successes during the day were claimed by both sides. It wag believed, however, that the chief honours rested with the Northern force. Colonel Mainwarine was assisted by Captain R S Oxley, D.A.A.G.. Captain A Evans- , Lombe, and Captain R L Hartley, Liverpool Regiment. With the exception of a little rain in the early morning the weather was fine, but the high wind add ,c 1 much to the difficulties of the cyclists. Considering the heavy rain which had fallen so recently, the roads were not in bad condition. Officers commanding companies gener- ally expressed the opinion that excellent work had been done, and that much instruction had, in the three days' operations, been gained hymen under their command:

The chairman remarked at some length on the much improved condition of the school in general. He was very pleased indeed to inform all present that woe a making there was an increase in the teachers of three over ithe pl-evious year and an increase in scholars of 25, which Was very good, They had tilso formed rnrina brass band,which he was pleased to say w very good progress under the able leader hip of mr Little the school senie•ary. div.head: NORTHERN UNION COMPETITION.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION COMPETITION.
LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETI- TION.
SATURDAY'S GAMES.
Warrington v. Mlnom.

The return match hctwsen these clubs took I.lace at Wprrington, before 5,000 spectators. Warrington, who ' w, re without Fish and Bate, kicked off, and bad a eight breeze behind them during the first half. A passing bout by almost the whole of the Warrington backs nearly gave Rateliffc an opening, but Young was the barrier. A score, however, soob came, for Lawless taking the ball at top spAsd gave it to Harris, who dashed over. Ratcliffe tailed at goal. Warrington again swarmed on the Millorn line, and Harris soon added a second try. S ill keeping op the attack,Warrington were almost over again, but offside play by Warrington give hfillom a footing in Warrington territory, and Eager' had an abortive shot at goal. Warrington were soon at their old position, and after a splendid run Isherwood scored a try, which he fail, dto improve. Scarcely had the ball been set in motion again when a forward dribble gave Taylor a chance, and be scored on the aide of the posts. Harris kicked a goal. Half time arrived with Warrington leading by one goal and four tries to nil. Swift restarted, and Millom shaped even worse after the interval, and scarcely ever did they even reach the half way line. At length, Fell, following up a dribble, took the ball out of Eagers' bands, and had a walk in behind the posts. Isherwood kicked a goal. Soon after the start from centre Isherwood dropped for goal,and added two more points. Result :—Warrington, two goals and five tries (21 points) ; Millom, nil.

div.head: Runcorn v. Widnes.
div.p: Runcorn v. Widnes.

At Runcorn Aspey kicked off for Widen. Whines for some time kept the home team in their own half, and Douglas, getting possession from a scrummage, gave to Lomax, ho was tackled by Houghton. From the next scrummage Jolley gave to Inglesfield ; the latter kicked across, and Lomas misfielding, Richardson picked uo and scored, but Jolley failed at goal. Passing by the Runcorn backs ended in Inglesfield scoring, no goal resulting. A dribble by Widnes was well taken by Hampson. He passed to Moss, who scored, but Bstey failed at goal. Halftime score : Runcorn, six points ; Widnes, three. Farmer restarted for Runcorn, and play rested in the Widnes half, but a kick by Batey;took play into the Runcorn quitters. By forward work the home team reached the Widnes quarters, and, Ts) lor kicking to Richardson, the latter dropped a goal, Soon after the restart Ilitey failed to field the ball, and several of the Runcorn backs dribbled away,which ended in Ingles- field scoring, and the same player kicked a goal, After this reverse Widnes went away, but could not penetrate the Runcorn defence. The Widnes backs fielded the ball very badly durina the latter portion of the game. Jolley was injured, and had to be carried off the field, Douglas marked near the Runcorn goal, but Bitev failed. Result —Runcorn, two goals and three tries (13 points) ; Wid- nes, one try (three points.)

Oldham v. Salford, At Oldham. Griffiths started for Salford, and within the first few minutes the visitors were penalised close up to their own goal line, and a score seemsd certain. Hnzzey took the kick, but failed. Resuming, both sides took their turn at attack, but success rested with the home side, S. Williams completing a neat movement between Lawton, Fletcher, Davies, and himself by scrambling over at the corner. Ferguson failed at goal. The succeeding play was of a rough and tumble char- ac'er, without much back play, and the only additional points scored were a couple made by a penalty kick at goal, in which Huzzey was successful. At the interval O'dharn were five points to the good. The Salford attack, however, was so vigorous, especially as played by the forwards, that, on changing ends, it was gener- ally felt that the game was not won. Hadwen and Williams, of the visiting backs, made their presence felt in several brilliant dashps, and Salford bad most of the play in the ePcond portion of the game. Oldham's de- fence was thoroughly sound, Fletcher and Thomas being conspicuous, and the utmost efforts of the visitors failed to cross the home line, and the game ended ia a win for Oldham by one goal and one try to nil. Swinton v. Rochdale Hornets. This match, played on the Athletic Ground, Rochdale, drew an attendance of about 5,000 spectators. At half time neither bad scored. Upon resuming in the second portion, the visitors were quickly the aggressors, and the Hornets for a considerable time were pressed, but they defended their lines. At length, from a drop out kick, Jones gained possession and ran in a try for Swin- ton, but Messer failed at goal. From another attack Wallwork got the ball from a pass by his centre and added another try for Swinton, but no goal resulted. IResult :—Swinton, two tries (six points) ; Rochdale Hornets, nothing.
Wigan v Stockport.

At Wigan before 3,000 spectators. Scrummaging enaued near the line.and on a break up WG,rsley cleverly made his mark, Oram landing a goal just on the interval Bali-time score: Stockport, one goal Wigan nil. Long kicking gave Wigan a footing at the other end. and, Stockport being ponalised,Brown equalised the scores by kickirg a goal. Following the resumption the game was keenly contested. both sides striving for further points. Eventually Bothwell made his mark,and Nelson kicked a goal. In the last minute Rigby scored and Nelson converted. Result :—Wigan, three goals and one try (nine pinta) ; Stockport, one goal (two points).

div.head: MONDAY'S MATCHES.
div.p: MONDAY'S MATCHES.
Warrington V. Leigh.

Warrington's concluding match in the Lancashire Senior Competition was with Leigh at Warrington on Monday, and the homesters wound up the season in handsome fashion. Leighbburt.,augphotwaefrufullitevaimad, bbultowWianrg- rington were short of Flab, Lawless -filing the vacancy. nwen the d weathergroul9nrevi redye r y much with the course of the game. 151 r Ashton of Werneth was the referee. and the teams lined out as follows : Warrington : Hallam, full-back ; Lawless, Isher- wood. Dickenson, and Harris, three-quarters; It Bate and Duckworth, half-backs ; Boardman, Morrison. Fell, Edmrndson, Mereweather, Scholtzt, Swift, and Eden, forwards.

Leigh (to come). Warrington lost the toss and Leigh at once attacked with the wind in their favour. Hallam early conceded a minor point. Lawless intercepted a Leigh pass and ran well to the other enc‘, Duckworth almost getting over at the corner. Dunbavin quickly sent Warrington back with a long puet, and Leigh attacked again. lkfolsineux passed to Dunbavin who spoiled a good opening for Davies by selfishness. A free kick against Warrington looked ominous, but Towers failed from an easy position. Bad kicking by the visitors lost them many opportunities, and the borne defence remained intict. A fine dribble by the home front rank rinsed another incursion into the Leigh half, Dickenson tusking a fine effert to get clear. Hallam misfielded a punt to the line, but Barrie snapped up the ball and ran powerfully to the quarter flag. Dunbavin dropped for goal from another penalty but failed and it looked odds on a blank score sheet at the interval, 9. minute from half time, however, Davies dashed in at the corner from a quick pass and Leigh crossed over leading by a try. On restarting. Duckworth took play to the Leigh quarter with a lofty kick. Warrington heeled out and the backs at once contributed a fine passing run which failed through the ball being intercepted almost on the line. Warrington played a more scientific game with the wind than Leigh bad done, and Harris was grassed jut outside after a strong effort. Isherwood picked up cleverly and threw across to Lawless who badly knocked-on at the corner. Leigh worked their way to the cebtre. and a piece of foul play caused Adereweather Ito be laid out. He took no furti.er part in the game. The Warrington forwards showed their appreciation of his loss by immediately dashing down the field,Morrison neat'y tipping the ball across for Dickenson to 1 score under the posts. Isherwood kicked a goal and gave Warrineton the lead. Though not eetting the ball as often Warrington kept up the attack with good pass- ing, rowers saying his charge pluckily on one occasion. Hate, Duckworth, and Isherwood cleverly exchanged again, and the latter dodged over finely near the goal. Ile took the kick himself, and successfully piloted the ball over the bar. Warrington now eased off a bit, and illivnley ran the ball to centre, the visitore front rank rushing to the line. Hallam sent them back with a penalty kick. Leigh struggled hard and attacked several times, bat the home defenders kept cool and easily repelled the invasion. Vinal Warrington, 2 goals, 2 tries (10 points) ; Leigh, 1 try (3 points).

div.head: Widnes V. Wigan.
div.p: Widnes V. Wigan.
Lea)

At Widnes, in boisterous weather. Widnes had a strong wind in the first half, and Hannon soared two tries. Rouse (Wigan) was off injured all the first half but resumed at the interval, and scored a try, flan followicg with two others in quick succession. After. wards Wigan pressed, but could not add to their lead. Result --Wigan, three trim; Widnes, two tries.
Runcorn v. Rochdale Hornets.

At Runcorn on Eater Monday. This was the last sague match of the season for Runcorn. Each team was fairly representative. The Hornets had the advan- tage of a very strong wind and a brilliant SUR behind them, but notwithstanding were on the defensive for half an hour out of the forty minutes. The Runcorn men displayed some of the form which enabled them to so handsomely defeat Swinton. A passing bout in which all the backs took part landed the ball to Inglesfield who scored a magnificent try, Jolley failing at goal. Then Runcorn forwards rushed the ball over the line and Lightfoot scored a second try, and at the interval Run- corn led by sir points to nil. Turning round Runcorn had the advantage of the wind, and play was of a very one-sided description. Tries were scored by Butterworth (quite in his old dashing style), Farmer, Inglesfield ard Jolley. Farmer placed three goals and Houghton added a fourth from a mark. In the end Runcorn won with great ease by four goals 6 tries (26 points) to Rochdale Hornets, nothing.

div.head: Barrow v. Swinton.
div.p: Barrow v. Swinton.

At Barrow, in fine but windy weather, before a large attendance of spectators. Barrow woo the toss. Evans started, and to return being made, Swinton invaded, but lost ground with touch kicks. Barrow pressed in- side the Swinton quartrr line, Swinton conceding a minor. Swinton passed finely. Davies making a fine opening, but limber forced Chorley to give another minor. Barrow were playing with great vigour, hut at half-time neither side had scored. In the see ond half Barrow played up pluckily, and kept their formidable opponents out until two minutes from time, when Swinton scored an unimproved try. Result; Swinton, three points ; Barrow, nil. Milicom v. Oldham.

A number of excursionists from Oldham visited the Millnm ground on Monday, and there were about 1,500 spectators present when Millom kicked off. Arthur Lees and Davies were absent from Oldham, bat billion' were also short of three regular men. Oldham played with a very strong wind. The Millom forwards played strongly, and Ti omits had to Rave. Oldham then had a turn,and Huzzev missed a penalty kick in front of the posts A try by Williams was the only score at the interval. Millom pressed sPVPrPII7 in the second half and Eagers just missed at VAL Northmore almost scored. but the result left Oldham winners and champions by one try to nil.

div.head: Champions v. Rest of Lea Tue,
div.p: Champions v. Rest of Lea Tue,

The Lancashire committee met in Manchester on Tuesday night, and selected the Rest team for this match at Oldham on twit 20: --Houghton (Runcorn), full back; Williams (Salford), Hogg (Broughton Ran- gers), R Valentine (Swinton), arid Fish (Warrington). threequarter backs; W James (Broughton Rangers) and Davies (Swinton), half-backs; Thempscn (Broughton Rangers). Vigors (Swinton), Treweeke (Barrow), M'Masters (Leigh). Walker (Ruleorn), Trotter (Stoe- port), Tunney (Salford), and Brown (Wigan), forwards. CHESHIRE JUNIOR CUP.

Runcorn Hornets v. Latchford Rangers. The clubs met in the semi-final of the Cheshire Junior Cup at Runcorn on Good Friday. The match was in- teresting and lively. .13,th teams played good open football and there was much excellent passing. A smart piece of work enabled Woods ti score a try for the Hornets and Moulton kicked a goal. The Rangers made desperate attempts to draw level, but could not pierce the defence and retired defeated but not disgraced by five points to nothing.

Begging at Stockton Heath. At the Warrington Occasionid Court, on Monday, before Mr. bionics, Patrick Connolly, who has been convicted of felony no fewer than 18 times, was charged with begging on the Grappenhall-road, , Stockton Heath, on Sunday afternoon, and was committed to gaol for 14 doss. Sergeant Bourne ' proved the case, Boat Race on the Mersey. The opening race for this season in connection with the Bank Quay sailing Club took place on Saturday, the course, being as usual, from Widnes, round a moored buoy near Walton arches, and back again to the east end of Monks,liall and Company's old quay wall. The competing boats and captains were the Conhie, Captain J Gleave ; Nymph, Cap- tain R Burthem ; Mephisto, Captain 11 Burthem ; Peggy, Captain J Kendrick; and the Wildflower, Captain H Warburton, The Connie was first away, followed by the MepAsto and Nymph, the Peggy fourth,and the Wildflo war whipping in. At Fiddlers Ferry,the Nymph had taken the lead,with Mephisto second, Connie third, Peggy still fourth. The 111ephisto,was first to the turning buoy, followed by Nymph, Peggy, Wildflower, Connie being last, and now began toe exciting part of the race, as it was a heat against wind and tide. The Wildflower now took the lead, and looked like winning,but she had to give way to the Peggy, with Mephisto coming on in fine style; the Nymph being fourth, and Connie last. Mephisto, took the lead 200 yards from the winning post, end kept, it, winning easily. The Nymph secured second place, Wildflower third, Peggy fourth, and Connie last. A Wedding Gift for Sir Gilbert Greenall. At the meet of the Belvoir Horind,a'at Little Poe. ton Hall, Grantham, Sir Gilbert Greenall,- Bart., the Master of the Hunt, was the recipient of a handsome present, consisting of two massive silver vases and a silver salver of Queen Anne model, sub- scribed for by 160 of his friends and supporters in the Belvoir Hunt, to commemorate his marriage, which took place on the 25th October last. The presentation was made by Sir Charles Welby, CB, MP. in the presence of a very large gathering, Sir. Charles Wslby said the subscribers most heartily and cordially wished Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall long life and plenty of happiness, and good sport in the Belvoir country. They were plessed to seize that opportunity of assuring Sir Gilbert of their gratitude and their appreciation of the way in which he had hunted the country. They hoped that for many years to come Sir Gilbert would con- tinue to enjoy and show good sport in that country they all loved so much. (Cheers). Sir Gilbert Greenall, in reply, said it was a great pleasure to receive the present, not only for its great value, but because it represented the feeling which existed and he trusted would always exist, between him- self and the members, the landowners, and the farmers of the Hunt. (Cheers )

div.head: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
[By " OvaHeti

For the first time in my immediate rec,llection War- ington have won three matches in rine week end. I can remember many occasions on which the local club has had three engagements in four days, and when our hopes of a triple success have been rudely dashed to the ground —often at the last moment. The Warrington team seems to have struck a vein of succe.,s just now and the gallant fifteen found ott apparent difficulty in aggregat- ing such a magnificent total as 55 points against Mamaingham, Minolta and Leigh during the Easter week end. All that the oi.position obtained was a solitary try, which stands to the credit of Monday's visitors, the Leigh Club.

By the defeat of the latter Warrington have completed their League programme and now stand sixth in the table of results with an aggregate ef 27 points out of 26 matches,a total they have only had once before equalled since the formation of the Northern Union and never yet surrassed. But for poor displays during the greater part of the season—and displays too which did not cor- rectly indicate the ability of the team--Warrington would probably have finished somewhere in the neigh- bourhood of th:ir Runcorn neighbours, who occupy the third position. Nobody is inclined to grumb e much now, however, all hopes being centred in the capture of the Northern Union and West Lancashire Cups as a fitting climax to the recent brilliant performances of the team.

Warrington were able en rest several players in the Millom match, but the team was still strong enough to win by 21 points to nil, and the narrow defeat at Millom was thus amply atoned for. I think the Millom men must have been saving their energies tor Oldham on Monday, as they did not appear to exert themselves overmuch after Warrington had scored. Harris die. tinguistied himself greatly in this match by scoring two fine tries and also placing a goal. Toe tries were genuine examples of what can be done by determination and dash. Some referees would have judged the scorer " held" on one occasion when he broke loose and scored after being tackled.

Isherwood was the hero of both Saturday's and Mon. day's games for he got seven points out of each by sterl- ing fwtbali, I question whether there is a better all. round man occupying the centre position than Isher- wood as he is at present. His own and Fish's prolific, scoring are strong testimony on behalf of this conten- tion. There is nothing showy about the skipper's play, but it is sound. I hope he may be rewarded by bringing home the cup, or cups.

Leigh came to Warrington on Monday, fully intend - lug to repeat their sunccesses of the past three seasons, a rid to demonstrate at the same time that the West Lancashire cup was practically theirs. They certainly looked a smart lot as they tripped on the sward in full strength, gaily bedecked in new jerseys. Luck favoured them in the matter of the toss, and with such a gale behind them they ought to have done better than score a solitary try one minute from the interval. Oa changing ends Warrington soon showed their mettle and rattled up ten points in very quick time, though Mereweather was absent as the result of a deliberate piece of violence by a Leigh forward. Leigh were well-beaten, especially in 019 back division and they will perhaps look upon the only cup in which they are interested with more longing than confidence in consequence.

Dunbavin and Molyneux are a renowned pair of half- backs, but they do not find favour in my eyes and would be no assistance to a niub !Ike Warrington. They rely too much on themselves and neglect the really capable three-quarter line behind them. Drop-kicking and punt- ing do not always win games, and on Monday they loa Leigh many chances in the first half. Davies and Ganley were good on the outride, and Towers played pluckily at full back. Bate and Duckworth were a much more affective pair behind the pack and they never failed to get the three-quarters going in a style which got points. Lawless was only a poor substitute for Fish, Dickenson and Harris being in fine form again. Hallam was moderate at full back. The forwards were splendidid in the loose, Morrison being the pick.

Should Widnes lose at Leigh to-day they will play St. Helens at Warrington on Monday for the honaur of escaping a fight with Morecambe, who aspire to pro- motion.

It is rather interescing to compare Warrington's pre— sent record in the League with the figures at the close of the 1396-97 season, when the same total of 27 points was reached. The present season must be considered much the more successful of the two for this time we finish one place higher in the league that in 1897, and the scoriag average is decidedly better. In that year, for instancs, the team only scored 12 goals, 16 tries, 100 points, according to the old reckoning—a total which Fish himself has easily passed this season. However, here ate the comparative records.—

To-day Warrington are confideotly expecting to enter the final stage of the Northern Union Cup Competition at the expense of Castleford, who ought, acc3rding to all the prophets, to suffer the fate of the five ocher Yurkshire clubs who have tried conclusions with War- rington this Feason. It is a great advantage to the Warrington men to play at Broughton on a ground on which they invariably give a gor4 display and where they are deservedly popular with the crowd. Not only that, the journey is so 'Short that a few thousand War- ringtonians may be expected to follow the team and give the players the usual encouragement of the " howl- ing oervish " chorus. This alnue is an important factor in success, according to one writer who reckons "to know you know."

Comparisons may be odious, but in football they are deridedl3 interesting. Ju.t. compare the figures below. which represent Castleford s performances in the York- shire League, with those of Warrington higher up. For. Apt. P. W. L. D. G. T. P. G. T. P. P. As the Castleford club is also second from the bottom surely the odds may tairly be considered in Warrington's favour.

Warrington will be fully represented in to-day's semi-final, Fish being pronounced "fit "once more. The selection is as follows. Hallam, full back ; Fish, Isher- wood, Dickenson. and Harris, threequarters ; p. Bate. and Duckworth, half-backs; Boardman, Morrison, Fell, Edmondson, Swift, Scholtze, Eden, and Cunningham, forwards. Mereweat her is, of alum injurcd, but be was not playing in his best form and will scarcely be mimed.

Still another comparison. 1 have been looking up the files of tbe "Examiner" •nd find that of the players who did duty for Warrington in the semi final at Hudders- field against Batley on April 24, 1897, only two are in. (Added in to-day's team, viz., Isherwood and Scholtse.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS

The usual meeting of the above Board, was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday. Mr J Moseley Williams preaided,and there were also preeent : MessrS Alt Norman, and Thomas Reynolds (Runcorn), the Rural District Councillors, with Mr George F Ashton (clerk), Mr W E Bough (assistant clerk), and Joseph Cuonah (master).

GIFTS FOR THE INMATES. The Master reported gifts of toys, for the inmates. from Mrs Leigh, Belmont Hall, Budworth ; and of doll dressed by the candidates of the Girls Friendly Society from Miss Whiley, and Mrs Willett, Stretton.—Votem of thanks were accorded the donors on the motion of Mr A R Norman.

CABSOL/C A POISON. The Local Government Board forwarded a copy of an Order of Council declaring carbolic acid a poison, aad approving a resolution passed by the Pharmaceutical Society ot Great Britain that liquid preparations of car- bolic acid and its homologues containing more than 3 per cent of those substances should, except in certain cases connected with agriculture and horticulture, be deemed poisons within the meaning of the Pharmacy Act, 1868.

THE DISTRICT AT/DITOR. The Local Government Board torwarded copy of an order declaring that Mr Walter Young, who recently acted :as deputy auditor, had been promoted to district auditor for the Notth-W3steru Audit District of Poor Law Unions.

PROTECTION OF INFANT LIFE. The Clerk submitted the third annual report of the Joint Committee appoin ed by thr Boards of Guardians of tne Chor!ton, Manchester, and Prestwich Unions to superintend the arrangments for onforcine the provisions rif the Infant Life Protection Act 1897, within the three Unions.

THE RETIRING CHAIRMAN. Mr Moseley Willie ins,at the conclusion of the ordinary business referred to the honour conferred upon him three years previously when be was appointed Chair- man. He felt that during that time they had treated him with the greatest indulgence and kindness. During, his three years of office, be might say they had been a very happy family. (Hest-, bear.) Any how. he did not remember anything, of what be might call the burn- ing (matfett '' :character, or a single personality being indulged in,-,-(bear, hear,)—neither had there been any introduction of anything of the nature of politics or religion. (aear, bear.) They might congratulate themselves on that score, and also on the fact that they found' ' the workhouse and its inmates in a far better condition as regards comforte than they fount them wh-n be first became a Guardian. A great many little cornices had been provided. The general administration of the Workhouse was infinitely better than it was a few years ago. The publio would be glad to know ,that, and also that their moley had been well spent.

Mr, Wright proposed a vote of thanks to the Chair. man for the able and expeditious way he had conducted the business of that Bwird. He had allowed full dis- cussion in the room, and he had been the right man in. the right place. Mr. Woodward seconded :—Carried. Mr. Williams responded. Mr. Limiter then moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Stokes, the vice-chairman. When appointed to that position he said he would do his.best to attend when Mr Williams was absent. He had carried out his promisele the letter. He had discharged the duties very efficiently. Mr. Moseley-Williams secondel. He had never known, Mr. Stokes to be backward in filling his place when he acquainted him of his inability to be present. The motion was approved.
