div.p: Lettero to the Moe. NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.
Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor.

Mattera intended for pubiicajon must be written on one side on 4 of the paper and sent in. if possible, not latter than Thursday. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short letter has much greater chance of insertion than a long one. We cannot under ordinary circumstances under- . .. .
take to return the nuauscripts which are not u3e3.
" Mercury " and the Trades Council.

Sir,—Your correspondent "Mercury " has not im- proved his position by his second letter. Evading any acknowledgment of his mistake in his first letter, viz "That Warrington returns nice Guardians," he makes another statement to the effect that from the reports of the Trades Council meetings he has noticed the names of a large number of insurance agents. Now, sir. I challenge " Mercury" to prove his statement- I assert there has not been more than one delegate of the In- surance Agents Society speaking at any of the meetings for at least two years. " Mercury's" idea of a Trades and Labour Council is somewhat belated and old-fashioned. There was a time when Trade. Unionism was narrow and intolerant, but like all other organizations who are progressive, they realize now that all who have to work for their living. and to do so must obtain work from an einnloyer, are truly and really labourers. They are subjected to the same conditions ; they must obtain work or starve. Any branch of labour therefore shows wisdom in uniting to obtain fair hears and wages for their work; no matter whether they are travellers, clerks, shop assistants, ko- Aad by the way, let me say if there are any branches of labour in which org,anizatioa is needed, it is in the two latter, for the conditions of work and pay of the bulk of the men and women engaged therein, are pitiable in the extreme. "Mercury" will see it is therefore perfect- ly within the scope of a Trades and Labour Council to receive any organisation of workers who have learned that unity is strength. "Mercury" speaks of the legitimate enterprise of the Council. What is legitimate for labour ? Anything tending for its betterment and uplifting. Is there anything of more interest to labour than the constitution of the Board of Guardians and the methods of relief in cases of poverty ? Seeing that working people are the great majority of those who have to seek relief, it is perfectly obvious that members of their own class, who know the conditions of their life, ought to b 3 on that Board. Sir, personally Ido not think it is wise or safe for any local authority to be composed of any one class, but Warrington being a typical working class constituency should have repre- sentatives of that class on every board or authority. As regards the elective auclitorship, Mr Flanagao was run by a number of working men who paid his expenses. He attended the Trades Council and stated the case for his candidature. A resolution was passed that the Council support him This is termed "moral support" •,Mercure ' says this is not worth much. Well, if the working men of Warrington through oarelsioness,spathy or ignorance, do not use their opportunities it is not our fault. We are trying to educate them to use their power wisely. "Mecury" on the other handlseems to rejoice in the fact of this deplorable state of mind of his fellow - townsmen. The accounts of the Corporation have to be duly audited by a professional accountant but the law also says the ratepayers shall elect two audito,s—responsible to the ratepayers—who shall see that the rates are spent wisely and legally. Brains are not monopolised by any class and there are many working-men capable of dulfilling the duties of elective auditor. Some of the best results have been obtained in our country by eleetine working-men to this office. I invite " Mercury " to reconsider himself and approach these matters with an open mind and he may see CCM to change his opinion. lain sorry that "Mer- cury's" first letter—which inlmy opinion was misleading —was usei as an election leaflet in the recent B )wsey Ward Election for the purpose of returning to the Board of Guardi.ns a member of the Tra le whose liefl 3eDite.- on local bodies is too powerful already,—Yours etc., P.J.

Sir,—As"Mercury,"for obvious reasons,seems to have lost sight of the arguments th he himself advanced and is still desirous of airing his ignorance of Trade Union matters, and alio u icQurteouslv ignoring the correc- tion of his mistaken ideas, I consider that to argue the subject any further with him would not only be a waste of time, but no goad could be derived from attempting to enlighten him further. So far as I am concerned this subject is closet —Yours respectfully, . . _

Warrington, April 3rd, Light for Camden Chapel. Sir,—You would do a public service to the people of Runcorn, if you were to visit some of the places of worship in the town, and give a few hints from time Co time as to how they might be improved with regard to itc. It is not pleasant in these days when we are dependent rather upon the books placed in .our hands than upon our memories, to find that the lighting of the place is so bad as to make it almost impossible either to follow the hymn.s or the lessons. Very much to the front as an offender in this particular is Camden Wesleyan Church, Lowlands-road, a place very dear to the hearts of the worshippers who assomble there from Sunday to Sunday, but who feel that there is a crying need for many improvements if the plaea should prosper, as there is every reason it should. Imagine giving a ' warm invitation to a friond to attend such s place of worship, and that friend finding a place so inadequately lit up. The consequence is that much effort is wasted and the warmest supporters and adherents of the place discouraged. Surely if there is a lack of funds for the purpose of a little extra light, it would only be necessary to make the matter known in order to insure the necessary money being found. Of course the matter of lighting is only one of the many improvement's though perhaps the most important at the present time. Others will suggest themselves to any who may frequently attend the place.—Yours faithfully, "GRUMBLER."

div.head: De Wet's Mental Condition.
div.p: De Wet's Mental Condition.
CAPETOWN, WEDNESDAY.
According to the latest information General Botha is prepared to treat for peace on behalf of the entire Boar forces.

During his recent interview with De Wet the latter refused to surrender, but his demeanour satisfied General Botha that he was mentally irresponsible, and as De Wet has hitherto been the only obstacle to the conclusion of peace General Botha is now desirous of re-opening negotiations. It is expected that in the event of Botha sur- rendering De Wet will be easily dealt with, as his force is rapidly decreasing.

div.head: Departure of the Warrington Vo!Lin
div.p: Departure of the Warrington Vo!Lin
teers. - Embarkation at Southampton.

It was twelve noon on Saturday when the long Lon- don and North-Western Railway train conveying the Warrington and other volunteers selected for service in South Africa entered the dock shed at Southampton, a hearty cheer from those already arrived welcoming the Northerners. In twenty minutes all were on board the Norman, and, what was of great benefit to the men after • long railway journey, at 12.30 a good hot dinner was served to the 600 odd men abroad. Up to twelve thA rain fell in torrents. Afterwards it cleared, and at 4 30, when the ship sailed, the sun shone brilliantly. There was, however, a strong wind and a heavy swell that promised a rough start: Toe mln were in good spirits and their appearance was a credit ta the town. Whilst the contingent was entraining at Bank Quay Station, Warrington, a young woman named Mary Streech. a domestic servant liv in.; at 73, Catherine-street fell between a railway carriage and the platform. She became hysterical and complained of injuries to her legs and right side. She was taken to the ladies' waiting r mm, but it was found that she had sustained only a slight bruise. She was conveyed home in a cab.

The usual weekly m;s—tin—g. of the Earlestown and District P.S.A. Society was held in the Co-operative Hall on Sunday afternoon. Mr Williamson presi- ded, and vocal selections were given by Mr T Maclin and Miss Hall. Recitations were given by Miss Bertha Smith. BARLESTOW-N WESLEYAN CIiCELCII.

On Monday, the Young' Men't;.l3ll7le—Ciass in con- nection with the above church held their first annual picnic, a visit being paid to Morecambe. About 60 of the members and friends journeyed by saloons which had been attached to the 7.25 a.m. train from Earlestown. After a very tiresome journey, Morecambe was reached shortly before , eleven o'clock. The party immediately made their way to the Gordon Cafe where a splendid dinner was partaken of. After the meal, the aft rnoon was spent in various ways. Drives to Heysham and the surrounding districts attracted the majority of the party, although the Winter Gardens and the other places of amusement in the town CMS in for a gooaly share of patronage. Tea was served at the Gordon Cafe at 530 and Morecambe was reluctantly left behind at 7 20 p m„ Earlestown being reached soon after 10 o'clock. The outing proved such a huge success that it is almost certain , that the affair will be made an annual one. Tile] party saw Morecambe under entirely favourable ' conditions, a brilliant sun shining the whole of the I day, whilst the only thing that militated against their enjoyment was the existence of a very high wind, which however, lessened in force as the after- noon went on. The whole of the arrangements were effectually carried out by the secretary, Mr. 0. Pickett. HAsTlint HOLIDAYS AT EAULESTOWN AND NE vToN

The weather in this neighbourhood was anything but favourable to holiday-making Choi Friday was certainly the best of the days, and every advantage was taken of Ghia fact by many pe,ople to take long walks into the country. Cyclists were out in hun- dreds and the main roads through Newton and on to Winwick were literally alive with wheelmen and women, who appeared to thoroughly enjoy the spring like weather. A very large number of people paid a visit to the Earlestown football ground, where the Earlestown Band was in attend- ance. A match was played between the local club and Little Halton United, and after the game danc- ing was indulged in until dusk. Saturday was a miserably wet day, and although the afternoon was fine,the weather was dull and threatening. In spite of this a large number of people left the town for vArions popular places of resort. The usuel Easter services were held at the various plac is of worship, and at one or two some slight decoration had ben indulged in. Monday opened early beautifully fine but about eight o'clock heavy threatening clouds came over and rain began to fall in torrents There was also a loud peal of thunder, and the wind veer- ing round to the south-west blew very strongly which about 11 o'clock had the effect of clearing away the vaporous clouds. The sun broke out and for the remainder of the day,the weather was of a beautiful description and all that could be desired. The trains during the morning were well filled, a very large number of people journeying to Liver-I pool and Manchester. About eight o'clock rain I began to fall again and continued without inter- mission during the night. All the works with the exception of the Printing Works were closed during the holidays, but operations were recommenced on Tuesday morning, although many of the men ap- peared inclined to have an extra day. The Rev J Carson, presided, but there was only a moderate atten lance. The chairman said they were doubtless all aware of the movement which was going on with regard to the renovation ot the church. They had had various opinions as to what shouldibe done,but no decision had been arrived at. So far as he could learn, the expense they should have to go to would be something like £3OO The exterior of the church was in fairly good condition, the organ should be taken down and cleaned and put up again and he hai reason t 3 belisite,that their exeellent organist and choir woad proceed to collect for that specially. With regard to raising the £3OO, he thought if the parishioners would do their best in that direction, they could approach the patrons, Lord Newton. and other gen'lemen. fie should like to have some sugges- tions as to the best method to be adopted for getting in the amount needed.—Ur Critchley asked if it was neceioary to raise the Whole of the £3OO before c :mmencinic the work of renovation. He thought if they put tie work in hand, sufficient guarantors could he found for the money —The Rector said if he saw a fair prospect of getting the money, he would like to have the work begun in the school holidays, say about the second week in July.— :Various ideas were put forward for raising the money, but none appeared feasible.—Mr Porter pro- posed that the wardens and sidesmen be a com- mittee to take the matter in hand, and that a cir- cular be drawn .up and issued to tho parishioners and others, setting forth the obi ects and appealing for donations.—This was s Aconded and unanimously carried.—Mr Critcniev brought forth a suggestion with regard to the choir being screened from the congregation—There were several dis.entients, but Mr Jos-ph Williams supported the 6uggestion.—The R ector said that he was in sympathy with the sug- gestion, and promised that it should receive con- sideration when they were in a position to proceed with the renovation-

The ordinary receipts for the year were rather less than usual, but the special collections were more. Of course if they had more collections for special purposes the ordinary receipts would 'suffer. He bad take' the trouble to work out the average of the ordinary receipts and he bound that this year the average was larger than it had ever been before. The reason why the ordinary receipts decreased was because they had had fewer Sun- days to collect on. He was very pleased to see that for the clergy fund they had contributed this year £46, which was an increaee on last year of 211 164. The 'collections on behalf of the choir had also increased. St. James' Church. This vestry meeting was held in the school on Tuesday evening. Tne Rev F E Powell (vicar) presided, and there was a large attendance of parishioners. ELECTION OF VICAR'S WARDEN. The Vicar remarked that for two years he had ben fortunate in having his friend Mr G Venn as his warden. He had done his work loyally and well, and had performed his duties not only to his (the Vicar's) satisfaction, but the satisfaction of the members of the congregation. It was a strong temptation to mix him to again undertake the duties of the position. He did not know wkother he would have accepted the office, but be (the Vicar) felt that to tie the office to any one individual was not altogether satisfactory from the standpoint of the pariih. Much as he regretted parting with Mr Vmn, be had decided to nominate another gentleman who had kindly intimated his willingness to accept the position, Flo had great pleasure in nominat- ing Mr Et N Houghton. Ho had been a member of the congregation for a comicierable length of time, and everyone kne.v the deep interest he took in church work generally, and in the welfare of St. James' in particu lar. Mr Houghton accepted the position, and Mr Venn expressed his thanks for the remarks of the Vicar.

MARKETS AND CEMETERY COMMITTEE. DECREASE IN MARKET TOLLS. The committee reported that the receipts for tho market for the year ended March 31st, 1931, amounted Cu £265 9 71, and the expenditure to £264 9s 101, leaving a profit of 19s 91. They also submitted a table showing the comparison with last year. This reveals an increase of £3 3s 61, in rents of inside stalls, and an in- crease of £6 15s 91 in receipts from weighing machine. Tnere has been a decrease of £ll 7s, in rents of outside stalls ;of£3 Os lid in tells ;of 144 in receipts from fairground, and of 12s iin rents of market cottages. The net decrease on the year's working is £5 15s 21. The Market Superintendent reported to the committee that the dezrease in tolls was caused through several hucksters' carts not coming into town during tho winter months, and the decrease in the rents of ou'side stalls was en account of two stalls being vacant. Tho minutes were confirmed. FINANCIAL BUSINESS.—THE ESTIMATES. La on WANTED roe THE TEANSPORTER BRIDGE. The Finance Committee reported that a letter had been received from Messrs dilsop, Stevens and Co., solicitors, to the Widnes and Runcorn Bridge Co, stating that the directors of the company would be glad to receive the sum of £2OOO, being the agreed first payment. It was recommended that application be made to th, Public Woiks Loan Commissioners to lend the sum of £lO,OOO for thirty years to enable the Council to meet the sills in respect to the shares suhscribed under the Widnes , and Runcorn Bridge lictf9oo. _ .

Mr Imison moved that the minutes be canfirme I; also that a rate of 3's t3l in' the 2 be levied for thenext twelve months, to be coileoted In two half-yearly instalments of 13 9 I each. The estimates neon which the rate was based were as follows :—Estimated expenditure : sewerage, £lOO e repairs of highways, main road, £400; ditto, other roads, £715,;. reconstrtintion of footw.ve, £400; urinals, £l5; scavenging, £730; watering,.£loo; slaughter-houses, £75; liehting, £1,008.; nightsoll re- moval £850; market, including public clack, £330; fire brigade, including hydrants. -265 ; inspector and regle- tration of canal boats, 1325,; disinfecting, £lOO ; hospital, £2oo'; salaries of officers, £1,084 , establish- ment charges other than salaries, £200; election, £2O ; legal expenses, £2o'; public offiees, £2OO free public library, £lB4 ; technical instruction, £lB4 ; noti- fication of infectioui disease, £3O; annuities, £376 *. ditto, transporter bridge, half-year, £53 ; Interest on loans, £620 ; sinking funds, 02E0; private street works. annual instalment. £117; water department, Id in the £ —£36B ; total £9275. Estimated income :.'Market rents and toils, £255; slaughter houses' £45;. office rents £126; half sanitar:t inspector's salary, £62 103 ; sale of night- soil, £65 ; mail roads, £4OO ; private street works. Interest from owners, £245 ; interest on investments £lOO ; gennr+l district rate. Recoverable arrears, £27 ; sundries. £25,103 ; transporter bridge, interest for half year, £3O, proportion of salaries from other funds, £265 total £1,646, The estimated expenditure, together with £l2O of a deficiency at 31st March, 1901, made a total of £9,395. Deducting from this the estimated income of £1,646, the amount to be provided was. £7',749. A Penny in thee was estimated to produce £lB4, and 3161 in the £ would produce £7,728 Mr Irnison said he thought the estimates which were referred to fully justified the resolution for a rate of 3s fid in the £. The total estimated expenditure was 22,395 Ho should not be surprised to find when the census returns came out that that amount would represent something like 103 a head for every man, woman,. and child in their district. Then toey would have an income of £1,646, which would represent something like is Bd, a head leaving about 83 4d per bead to be provided by the rate for the general expenses of the Council: He did not think the public would be entirely unprepared for this increase. It had been seen durinz the past year that an increase was inevitable. One of the principal causes was connected with the water department. Owing to the very great increase in the esst of fuel the' expenses of that department necessitated the in- clusion of a sum of money in the rate to enable it to clear off its liability. Then again the nightsoil removal department had also been more expensive than had been anticipated. The same remarks applied to the hospital. The hospital buildings, they might remember were not in the very best condition of repair, and they felt that they had undertaken liability with regard to the Port Sanitary Authority that reqpireck some ade- quate provision being made in case at any time they were required to work under the contract they had entered into. The committee therefore determined that they would put the hospital into shape far meeting any: necessity that might arise during the coming year. They also meant to spend rather more on the hospital than had hitherto been included in the estimates for the pointing and painting of thiabuildings. They were als3 proposing to do necessary repairs. to the market and slaughter-house. He thought the ratepayers would con- sider that the Council were justified in incurring this expenditure for the reason that it was with the object of keeping their properties in good order. Although the rate was a burden, yet he believed the ratepayers were satisfied that the money was being well and wisely spent, and that they were receiv- ing full value for the money tell tired. The ratepayers might feel perfectly satisfied that the Council had been very determined to secure that proper value should be received for this larger expanditure. If the rate worked out as they hmed it would, they. would discharge their liabilities. He thought it was perhaps one of the most straight-forward estimates that had been presented to that Council. They were providing for all their estim- ated expenditure with the exception of 221, and they expected that the ordinary growth of the rate would enable them to discharge that obligation. Mr. &acid seconded. One regretted that in the present depressed state ef the town it as inevitable that an additional 3.1 should be placed upon the rate,but they had no other choice. Bethought that in the future, as far as they could, they ought to study economy in respect to the expenditure at the Common and other places, and endeavour as far as possible to stop the rate growing any larger. The minutes were confirmed. POSTM. ramerrtas ANII. LIGHTING. . . -

A suggestion was received from the Runcorn Post- master to the effect that the sub-offices in the district should be closed on Wednesday afternoons, as was the case elsewhere. The pillar boxes would remain open for theposting of letters as usual I Mr Posnett hought when a reply was sent the Coun- cil should ask that the lamp over the letter box at the General Post Office—which was provided by the Coun- cil for the public convenience-3hould be more brilli- antly lighted.

Mr Itnison. said this was distinctly a matter which needed attention. A farthing candle would give a better light than the one which was given at present. Ho was glad to hear that the local authority was Consulted in these matters, and he moved that a reply be sent to the effect that they agreed with the suggestion as to the closing of the sub-offices, but they protested against the imperfect lighting of the lamp at the head office. Mr Bisbrown seconded, and the motion was carried. THE PORT SANYPARY AUTHORITY. A NEW SCHEME OF REPRESENTATION PROPOSED. div.head: OLD FOLKS TREAT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: OLD FOLKS TREAT AT RUNCORN.

The usual treat given to the "Old Folk 'of Run- corn town, was held at the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Wednesday evening last, when some 350 per- sons over the ago limit sat down to a delightful banquet. The proceedings were taken part in by Mr w Handley J.P (chairrean of the District Cooncil), the Rev Canon Wood, MA, (vicar Rev A Wells (Wesleyan superintendent), Messrs S Taylor, JP, F J Norman JP, E Imison, CC, JP, M J S weetman, E Marshall, W Coventry. T Woods, J fimperley, W Shaw (missionary),George Howard, J W Lightourn (clerk to the School Board), J Rowles the members of the committee and many of' the leading tradespeople of the town. It was interest- ing to see the " old folk" happy in re-union,talking over "old times," to the interesting accompaniment of a good feast. The most aged person in their ranks was Mrs Mary Robinson who has attained her 91th year. Mrs Kershaw, another aged lady was perhaps the centre of interest, inasmuch as she enjoys the happy distinction of haying been born on the same day as her late Majesty Queen Vic- toria,the 24th of May,her age being 82 years. The tables were 28 in number and were presided over by :—Miss Crosby and Mrs Graham; Mrs F J Norman and Mrs W Leathwood ; Mrs C Leatbwood and Mrs T Cooke ; Mrs F Ellison and Mrs Dudley; Mrs Turner; Mrs R Morris; Miss Percivil (Church. street) ; Mrs Poynter; Mrs T Wood; Mrs H W Hand- ley and Miss Shaw; Mrs W Seaw, sea. and Mrs W Shaw, jun.; Mrs P Leathwood ; Miss Cameron; Miss Stubbs; Mrs T Reynolds and Mrs W J Timperley ; Mrs Bowyer and Mrs G Kirkham ; Mrs W and Mrs Coventry; Mrs Larkin ana Mrs Jolley; Mrs Roodes;M,B Imison; Miss Broadhurst and Miss Mellor Mrs R Moore and Miss Millington ; Ntiss Pearson; Mrs liailwood and Miss E Riley; Mrs D Littlemore ; Mies C Savage and Mrs Williams; Mrs 0 Howard; and Miss Wells. The ladies were in turn assisted by a corps of about 75 young people,who kindly as ed as waiters. 'I bus it will be seen that the old folks were not wanting in attention, An entertainment followed the tea,over which Mr W Handley presided (wearing his chain of offi:e), and he was supported by a number of the gentle- men already named. Addressing his old friends Mr Handley expressed the pleasure the promoters of the tteat felt at see- ing so many of them present. It had been thought by some of them better to have the treat in the warm - weather, and that was the reason it was i.neld _
, warmer

at the present time instead of in the winter months as previously, and the only regret they had was that more had not come. There were some- thing like 350 present, but some 460 tickets had been applied for and given out. However as it comes round another year they led that the gathering would be increased that all who were then present would be spared e, another year. (Hear, hear.) It'was a gather- og of old Runcorn people, and as he moved about imongst the tables he noticed a number whom he remembered from the time when be was duite a little lad—and that was a great many years ago. (Laughter). Taking his hearers back halt a cen- tury, he pictured Runcorn as it then was with its population o 8688 in 1851, and its few houses, and compared it with the town of the present day and Its population, which it was expected the census recently taken would show to be 20,000. They would remembbr that the very spot on which they were assemble I that evening was 50 years ago the place where the circuses and shows of the town were held. It was known as Walkers Croft, and they would remember too what a wonderful thing it waa considered when gas mains were laid to the spot for the purpose of lighting the shows at night- time. Runcorn was very different now from what it was then. But was Runcorn better or worse? He said that Runcorn was very much better. If they had progressed in numbers they ha I progressed in comforts too. There was not a working man to-day who was not better fed, better housed, and better clothed than he could possibly have been 50 or 60 years ago in Runcorn. (Hear, hear.) They had more comforts In every way. He always stuck up for Runcorn and It was remarkable how people who only came to live in the town always left it with regret, and in after years remembered it with great pleasure. (Hear, hear.) Runcorn was a good place and a ' homely place and he hoped they would all be proud ,of their native town as long as they lived. (Hear, hear.) Indeed he hoped it would always be with Ithem "Runcorn with all thy faults:l love thee still," and he trusted that all would do their best for their inative town,and to make Runcorn all the better for their having lived in it. (Applause.) The following programme was then proceeded with :—Part I. Mandoline solo, Miss L Temperley; song, "Mary," Mr T Withington; English concertina duet, Messrs Hendrick and Knight; song, "The New Kingdom," Miss E Clare; violin solo, "Romance in G," Mr T Stubbs; recitation," The Doctor and his ApprenticerMiss E Saunders ; song, "Alone on the raft," Miss Simkin : humorous song, "The Story of a Bike," encore, " Polly-wolly-doodle," Mr F Ellison. Part 11. Violin duet, "Spanish Serenade," Messrs Stubbs and Prince; recitation, Miss Saun- ders; mandoline solo, selected, Miss L Temperley : song, "fivickenhain Ferry," Miss E Clare ; Knglish concertina duet, Messrs Hendrick and Knight ; song, "Children's Home," Mr T Withington ; humorous song, "I'd like to go halves in that," en- cored, Mr F Ellison. The accompanists were Mr W Cooke, A.R.C.0., and Miss C Leathwood, and the piano used had been kindly lent by Mr William e haw, junior, Top Locks, Runcorn. During the interval the Rev A Wells sple encouragingly to the old folks, and recited Tom Hood's " Oh when I was a little boy." Mr Ralph Peacock, aged 77, and Mr Robert Brown, aged 83, proposed and seconded a vote of thanks to the donors of the treat ; to the ladies and assistants who attended them so well; and to the artistes for their entertainment, which was unani- mously carried. The two old gentlemen also sang a hymn as a duet, and were heartily applauded. The whole proceedings terminated with "God save the King." _
ooped and r' for 1 , ing

Messrs Ogden, of tobacco fame, kindly gave an ounce of tobacco 'o each of the old men, through their agent Mr It Moore, Church-street, and the committee presented a two ounce packet of tea to each of their old ladies; Messrs Yarwood and Booth provided cabs for the conveyance of the infirm back to their homes; and the Mersey Mission to Seamen kindly provided cro3kery along with others, all of whom the committee desire to thank. The official secretaries were Messrs George Howard and J Rowles; and the musical programme was got up by Messrs F Ellison and William Shaw, Jun.

OUR NEW SERIAL. OUR NEW SERIAL. We have pleasure in announcing that we have secnred for publication in our columns a thrilling Story entitled. "THE LADDER OF GUILT," BY ULYIS R'JGERS, Author of " Mims," "For Love end the Queen," " Wedded In Mystery," etc. Mr. ULYSS ROGERS. the author of our new story, contrary to the experience of most young authors. confesses to having met with a very kindly reception upon coming to London and placing his literary wares at the disposal of London editors. lie ascribes this success to the fact that as a provincial journalist he took years endeavouring to stud/ the exact requirements of the story-reading public before venturing to exhibit his productions for editorial criticisms. Mr. Rogers dOICIRE the three years he has devoted himself' to fiction has published several serial stories and some scores of short ones, contri- buting to practically all the popular London Magazines and weekly periodicals. " Mime." " For Love and Queen," and Wooded in Mystery." have galned Mr Rogers a reputation which will, Without doubt, be considerably enhanced by his latest serial, " THE LADDER OF GUILT." "THE LADDER OF GUILT." "THE LADDER OF Gunn " plunges the reader into the thick of the plot from the very eommenee- Utent, and the interest is maintained through every instalment. It is a story of love, of hate, and of the descending Steps in "the ladder of gulls" to which a weak- Minded man is led when once the balance of his life goes wrong owing to an unrequited affection. It is a story of country life and, also' to a great extent deals with prison experiences and systems' A Particularly sensational chapter is that in which the last penalty of the law is evaded in what might almost be regarded as a miraculous manner, were it not that fiction, in this case, as in most others, has a Wonderful counterpart in fact. To say more Narding this extraordinary passage would be but to 'Poll the reader's appetite and spoil the effect of the scene. THE LADDER OFGUILT." The opening chapters of this exciting Story appear in our columns. TO-DAY TO-DAY TO-DAY.

A LESSON FROM CALVARY. On Calvary the Saviour died, God's sinless Lamb by sinners slain While round the Cross His captors vied In mocking Him with cries profane. And 0, to screen from angels eyes That crowning act of human crime, An awful darkness veiled the skies, And hid the actors for a time. Yet full of love and pity still, No murmur stirred the victim's breath No cry for vengeance swift to kill The crowd that hungered for His death. Nay ; in that hour of snrow, dread, Reviled without, heart-sore within ; The dying Saviour raised His head, And prayed for pardon for their sin. 0 would that all who wield the sword, And in the guilt of carnage share ; By faith might see their stricken Lord, And grasp the spirit of His prayer. For surely, 0 most surely then. Tba horrid crime of war would cease ; And men respect their fellow men, Their only King, the Prince of Peace. But there is warfare still to do Against the powers of death and h°ll And all who would that war pursue, Muit know and love the Savir.ur well. For carnal weapons are unkown To these who mingle la that strife : Th- soldier armed with love, alone Ma; hope to a in the crown of life. J. H. W. CLINDINNA• Good Friday, 1901.
